# MSG gripper

> Documentation for the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper by Source Robotics.

Every page of this site is also available as Markdown at its address followed by `index.md`, with its links absolute; `llms-full.txt` holds every page in one file. The version box on the landing page names the release the pages describe.

Full text of every page, in the order of the site's navigation. Source: https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/

# MSG Gripper Manual

![MSG gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/hero.webp)

<div class="doc-meta" markdown>

**Document number:** SR-5003

**MSG gripper release:** 1.2

**Firmware:** STEPFOC 109

**Revision:** 2026.D

**Published:** 2026-11-10

**Applies to:** MSG gripper release 1.2 with the STEPFOC driver PCB v1, STEPFOC firmware 109

*Original instructions*

</div>

[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/quick-start/) [About this manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/about/)

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document for the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper. It is revised as the gripper and its
firmware change; the document number, the gripper release, the firmware, the revision and the date above identify
the version you are reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. The version selector
in the header switches between gripper releases. The gripper runs the STEPFOC driver's firmware: take care that
the firmware named under *Applies to* matches what the gripper reports. The text and the images are licensed
CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

**The MSG is open source, and that is important to us.** Everything the gripper is made of is published: the
CAD and print files, the bill of materials, the assembly instructions, the driver's firmware and the software that
drives it. Buy the gripper assembled, or build one yourself; change the jaws or the body for your application and
fit it to any robot. The [build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/) is the order to do it in.

**Made for teleoperation and robot learning.** We designed the MSG specifically for teleoperation, VLA
(vision-language-action) training and physical intelligence. The camera on top of the body is placed with care:
it looks down between the jaws at an angle that keeps both jaws, and the object between them, in view, the
picture a teleoperator and a learning model need.

<div class="gripper-viewer" data-base="assets/models/msg/" markdown="0">

</div>

# Quick start

From an assembled MSG gripper to its first gentle open and close, using Motor GUI on a PC.
For a gripper already connected to a robot, use [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/).

!!! danger "Before connecting power"
    Keep fingers and loose objects out of the stroke. Calibration opens and closes the jaws fully. A wrong
    cable can reverse the supply or put 24 V on a CAN pin, and either destroys the driver: check the [numbered pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/connector/#pin-numbers).

## 1. Choose your starting point

| Your gripper | Start here |
|---|---|
| Bought assembled | Its stepper is already calibrated and the driver configured. Continue below; the jaws still need calibration after each power-up. |
| Self-built, or a replacement driver or stepper | Finish [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/) first, then return here. Do not apply a factory preset to a bought gripper just to try this page. |
| No hardware yet | Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)** and **Connect**, then switch to **Gripper**. The demo is an SSG-48; the control panel is shared with MSG. |

## 2. Gather and mount

You need a mounted gripper with jaws/fingers fitted, a **24 V supply**, a correctly wired **M8 cable**, a
**CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter**, and Chrome or Edge. The [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/what-you-need/) page lists
the parts; [Mounting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/mounting/) and [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/) cover the mechanics.

!!! success "Check"
    The body cannot shift, the jaws travel freely, and the cable cannot enter their path.

## 3. Wire with power off

1. Check the cable against [Connector and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/connector/): gripper pin 1 is +24 V,
   pin 3 GND, pin 4 CANH, pin 2 CANL. Check continuity before the first power-up.
2. Connect the supply and the CANvas adapter as shown below.
3. Set the gripper's CAN termination ON for this two-node bench bus; the CANvas adapter provides the other end.
   Leave the gripper at its shipped node ID, **0**, unless you already assigned another.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PC[PC USB] --> A[CANvas adapter]
    A -- CANH --> P4[Gripper pin 4: CANH]
    A -- CANL --> P2[Gripper pin 2: CANL]
    S[24 V supply] -- positive --> P1[Gripper pin 1: +24 V]
    S -- return --> P3[Gripper pin 3: GND]
```

!!! success "Check, unpowered"
    The supply polarity and cable pinout match, and CANH-to-CANL measures about **60 Ω** with the bus connected.
    Otherwise check [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/) and [CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)
    before powering it.

## 4. Connect Motor GUI

Power the gripper, plug the CANvas adapter into USB, and open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/).
Choose **CAN (slcan)** at **1 Mbit/s**, press **Connect**, and choose the adapter's serial port.
Select node **0** (or your assigned ID) and switch from **Motor** to **Gripper**.

The [illustrated Motor GUI guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/motor-gui/) shows the panel.

!!! success "Check"
    Position and current feedback arrive. *Not calibrated* after power-up is normal. If feedback is missing,
    check the power, port, node ID and termination: [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/). If a fault
    disables the controls, resolve it using [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/).

## 5. Calibrate and activate

If the panel shows an error, press **Clear errors** first. With the stroke empty and the gripper deactivated,
press **Calibrate**, read the prompt, and press **Start calibration**. Let the jaws find both end stops, and
press nothing else until the panel says **Calibrated**: a move or a clear during the calibration ends it. Follow
[Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/first-moves/) for the full procedure, then **Activate** and check for
faults.

!!! success "Check"
    The panel says **Calibrated**, **Activated**, and **No errors** before you command a move. A calibration
    that times out after 24 seconds has not found its end stops; do not continue as if it passed. Use
    [Calibration troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/#calibration).

## 6. Make the first move

Set **Speed 30** and **Current 300 mA**, applying each with its **Set** button. Press **Open**, then **Close**.
After that works, put a light test object between the jaws and repeat, keeping fingers clear.

The current limit sets an approximate force limit; [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)
explains the relationship and the motor's limits.

!!! success "Check"
    The position follows the command; on an object the jaws stop before fully closed and the panel reports an
    object. If it does not move, slips or reports an error, use [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/).

## 7. Finish and continue

Remove the test object before deactivating or switching off: the grip may release. Disconnect Motor GUI and
switch off the supply before changing cables.

| Next task | Guide |
|---|---|
| Control it from a program | [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/), [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ros2/) |
| Put it on a robot | [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/) |
| Inspect a CAN frame or download DBC definitions | [CAN frame tool and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can-tools/) |
| Diagnose a problem | [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/), [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/) |

# About this manual

The MSG Gripper Manual covers the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper from unpacking to a gripper that works on a robot: mounting and cabling, the
first setup with Motor GUI, control over CAN and UART, from Python, from ROS 2 and from the PAROL6 and PAR6
robots, and firmware updates. It is written for a maker, a student or an engineer who can plug in a cable and run
a Python script. Read [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/02-safety/) before you power anything; [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/) is the
shortest path to a gripper that moves.

The gripper is a STEPFOC stepper driver in gripper mode. The driver itself, from its full command set to its calibration
and its bootloader, is documented on the [STEPFOC site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/); this manual links there instead of
repeating it.

## Finding your way

Four tabs: **MSG Gripper Manual**, the numbered chapters, read from the start; **API reference**, the gripper's CAN
messages, UART commands, status bits and Python calls, for looking things up (the driver's complete reference is on
the STEPFOC site); **Guides**, worked examples; **Support**, help and problem reports.

The dropdown next to the site name switches between gripper releases, and a page of an older release says so in a
bar at the top. The repository card in the header opens the product repository; every page ends with a link to
edit it and one to report a problem with it.
## Warnings and notes

!!! note "Note"
    Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

!!! warning "Notice"
    The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

!!! danger "Danger"
    Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.
## Related documents

|---|---|---|
| MSG Gripper Manual | SR-5003 | the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper: safety, technical data, installation, setup, operation over CAN, UART, Python and ROS 2, firmware, the build guide; the gripper's API reference; guides |

A document marked with a firmware release describes MSG gripper release 1.2 running STEPFOC firmware 109. The version selector in the header switches between gripper releases; a new firmware release for the same gripper updates the pages in place. The compatibility table says which firmware, Python library and hardware revisions work together.

The driver inside the gripper is documented at [https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/). The SSG-48 gripper, the MSG's predecessor on the Spectral Micro driver, is at [docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/). The robots the gripper is
made for: [docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/) and
[docs.source-robotics.com/par6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/).

## Document history

The manual is versioned by gripper release, the version the product repository tags (the selector in the header);
within a release it follows the STEPFOC firmware the gripper runs, with a new revision letter per update. The
text and the images are licensed [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), the code
examples [MIT](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-gripper-docs/blob/main/LICENSE-CODE); the hardware design is published under the CERN Open Hardware Licence v2, strongly reciprocal in the
[product repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper). The Source Robotics name, the product names and the logos are not covered
by any of these.

| Revision | Date | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.D | 2026-11-10 | STEPFOC firmware 109: the generated CAN and UART reference; the encoder table and the anti-cogging that follow `#Cal` in the first run, and the presets' gains on 109; a poll right after a move no longer cancels it (KI-10); calibration puts the current limit back (KI-5); the gripper's current clamped at 2800 mA. Python library 1.21, which reads the object detection right (KI-6) |
| 2026.C | 2026-11-05 | The M8 pinout corrected to the one the gripper is built with (1 +24 V, 2 CANL, 3 GND, 4 CANH; page 17 of the SSG-48 assembly manual): the pin table, its drawing and the quick start of 2026.B had all four pins wrong; the bootloader comes with STEPFOC release 105, not 104; the camera works with any webcam software; the cable warnings: the other robot's cable reverses the supply, it does not put 24 V on the CAN pins; the PAROL6 cable's pin pairs |
| 2026.B | 2026-11-04 | Gripper release 1.2, with the files as downloads on the release; dimension drawings and what changes per variant; data for robot integration (frame, mass, inertia, TCP); known issues; the downloads with their versions; safety for clothing, hair and eyes, a caught finger, static and cleaning; check boxes after each step and Windows, Linux and macOS tabs; numbered figure captions; the 380 g variant |
| 2026.A | 2026-11-03 | First version in this form: the manual chapters, the generated CAN and UART reference; gripper release 1.1, firmware 108 |

# Overview

What the MSG gripper is and how it works, the variants it comes in, and what you need around it to get it
gripping.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The gripper in action](https://img.youtube.com/vi/YUvNXfaHM6s/hqdefault.jpg){ width="480" }
  <figcaption><a href="https://youtu.be/YUvNXfaHM6s">The video of the gripper in action</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

## In this chapter

- [The gripper at a glance](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/gripper-at-a-glance/)
- [Variants](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/variants/)

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/gripper-at-a-glance/ -->

# The gripper at a glance

The MSG is a two-jaw parallel gripper driven by a NEMA 17 stepper under field-oriented control. The
[STEPFOC driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/) on the back of the stepper regulates the motor's
current, so a move sets not only where the jaws go and how fast, but how hard they press: the current limit is the
grip force. The jaws stop on an object, hold it with that force, and the driver reports that an object was found.
We designed the MSG specifically for teleoperation, VLA (vision-language-action) training and physical
intelligence. A camera on top of the body looks down between the jaws, from a place chosen for a clear view of
both jaws and the object between them.

![The MSG gripper with the 150 mm rail and the camera mount](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_banner.webp){ width="900" }

## The parts

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| NEMA 17 stepper motor, 21.5, 40 or 60 mm long | the actuator; its length sets the grip force: about 31, 50 or 76 N at its maximum current |
| STEPFOC driver on the back of the stepper | field-oriented control of the stepper, the gripper state machine, the CAN and UART interfaces |
| Pinion on the motor shaft, two racks on a linear rail | the pinion turns, the two racks move in opposite directions: the jaws open and close symmetrically |
| MGN7 linear rail, 100, 150 or 200 mm | carries the jaws; its length sets the stroke |
| Jaws | printed, in several shapes, with a soft TPU pad or solid; yours to adapt |
| Thermistor on the motor housing | temperature protection: the gripper stops at 75 °C |
| M8 4-pin connector | 24 V and the CAN bus, one cable to the robot |
| Camera mount | an OV9732 USB camera module looking between the jaws |
| Coupler plate | mounts the gripper on an 8 mm shaft, or on the PAROL6 wrist with its own cover |

The driver's status LED and its UART port are inside the housing; the CAN termination switch is reachable
through the stepper cover ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)).

## What the firmware does

After power-up the gripper calibrates by finding both end stops. Then it takes move commands: a position from 0
(open) to 255 (closed), a speed from 0 to 255 and a current limit in mA. When the jaws stop short of the target
with the current at its limit, an object is in the way and is held; when they reach the target, the position is
held. Every answer carries the state: moving, object found while closing or opening, or at the position. The
gripper stops itself on an over-temperature, an E-stop bit from the host, a CAN watchdog that runs out, and every
fault the driver detects. [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/) and
[Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/) have the details.

## How it is controlled

- **CAN**, 1 Mbit/s, on the same cable as the power: one message moves the gripper and is answered with its
  state. From a PC with the CANvas adapter, from a ROS 2 node, from PAROL6 or PAR6, or from your own controller.
  See [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/can/).
- **Python**, the `Spectral-BLDC` library on top of CAN. See [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/).
- **Motor GUI** in the browser: connect, calibrate, open and close, watch the plots. See [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/motor-gui/).
- **UART**, the driver's serial port inside the housing: for configuration, and for a self-built gripper. See
  [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/uart/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/variants/ -->

# Variants

The gripper is modular in two ways: the length of the linear rail sets the stroke, the length of the stepper sets
the force. Any rail goes with any stepper, and the body comes in black or grey; the body, the jaw carriers and the
stepper cover are printed for the chosen combination.

![The three rail lengths and the stroke each gives](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/Gripper_strokes.webp){ width="900" }

=== "Black"
    ![The nine combinations of rail and stepper, black body: 55, 105 and 155 mm of stroke across, the 21.5, 40 and 60 mm steppers down](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_variants_black.webp){ width="900" }

=== "Grey"
    <figure markdown="span">
      ![The nine variants, grey body](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_variants_grey.webp){ width="900" }
      <figcaption>The same nine combinations, grey body.</figcaption>
    </figure>

## Rail length and stroke

| Rail | Stroke | Printed parts |
|---|---|---|
| 100 mm | 55 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_100mm`, `gripper_jaw_100mm_L/R` |
| 150 mm | 105 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_150mm`, `gripper_jaw_150mm_L/R` |
| 200 mm | 155 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_200mm`, `gripper_jaw_200mm_L/R` |

The stroke is the distance between the jaw carriers from fully open to fully closed; the opening between the
jaw faces depends on the jaws you fit ([Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/)). A longer rail makes the gripper wider
and a little heavier and does not change the force.

## Stepper length and force

| Stepper | Motor | Maximum current | Assumed torque constant | Ideal combined force at the maximum current | Printed parts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm | 17HS08-1004S | 1.5 A | 0.17 Nm/A | about 31 N | `Stepper_cover_21_5mm`, `Stepper_spacer_21_5` |
| 40 mm | 17HS16-2004S1 | 2.0 A | 0.21 Nm/A | about 50 N | `Stepper_cover_40mm` |
| 60 mm | 17HS24-2104S | 2.1 A | 0.30 Nm/A | about 76 N | `Stepper_cover_60mm` |

A longer stepper gives more torque and so more grip force, at the price of weight and length behind the
gripper. The force is proportional to the current limit you command, with the slope of the stepper's torque
constant; the curves and the formula are in [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/). The
current limit must stay within the stepper's maximum.

## Grasps

The gripper grips from the outside (the jaws close on the object) and from the inside (the jaws open inside a
hollow object). Both are the same move command with a different target; object detection reports *while closing*
for the first and *while opening* for the second.

## The camera

The camera mount on top of the body carries an OV9732 USB camera module (100° version in the BOM), looking down
between the jaws. Its place and angle were chosen with care: the camera sees both jaws and the object between
them, the view that teleoperation and VLA training need. It is a plain USB camera with its own cable,
independent of the gripper's electronics: the computer sees it as an ordinary webcam, so any program that
reads one works with it, from the camera app to OpenCV (`cv2.VideoCapture`) in Python or a ROS 2 camera node. The
mount and its lid are printed parts (`camera extension`, `camera_lid`), and a gripper without a camera simply leaves
them off.

![The gripper on a PAROL6 and what its camera sees](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_and_camera.webp){ width="700" }


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/what-you-need/ -->

# What you need

## The gripper

The MSG gripper is sold assembled, calibrated and configured in the [Source Robotics shop](https://source-robotics.com/products/msg-gripper),
in the rail and stepper combination you choose, in black or grey. It ships with the current STEPFOC firmware and
the bootloader installed, its driver in gripper mode and its stepper calibrated; the gripper calibration (finding
the end stops) runs after every power-up and is part of normal use.

**Or build it.** The MSG is open source, and that is important to us: the CAD and print files, the bill of
materials, the assembly video, the firmware and the software are all published. [The build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/)
is the order to do it in.

## What is in the box

The gripper, assembled, calibrated and configured, in the rail, stepper and colour you ordered, with the camera
module when ordered. **Not in the box:** the jaws, which you print from the repository or buy in the shop; the
cable, sold separately; a CAN adapter for a PC.

## A cable and a 24 V supply

The gripper is powered and controlled through one M8 4-pin cable: 24 V, GND, CANH, CANL.

| Where the gripper goes | Cable |
|---|---|
| PAROL6 | the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) from the shop |
| PAR6 | the PAR6 gripper cable (the shop; coming soon), wired differently from the PAROL6 one |
| a bench, or your own robot | a cable you make from an M8 4-pin connector and four wires, see [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/) |

![PAROL6 and PAR6 gripper cables are not interchangeable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/cable_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

!!! danger "The two robot cables differ"
    PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. A cable for the wrong robot, or a self-made cable with
    a wrong pin, puts 24 V where the CAN bus belongs and destroys the gripper's driver. Check the pinout before
    you plug in a cable for the first time.

On the bench, a 24 V supply with a current limit (2 A is plenty for one gripper) is the safest source.

## A CAN interface

The gripper talks CAN. On a robot, the robot's control board provides the bus. On a PC, the
[CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) does; it shows up as a
serial port and works with Motor GUI, the Python library and the ROS 2 driver. Any adapter that `python-can` supports works
with the library.

## Software

- **Motor GUI**, [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/), in the browser over the CANvas adapter: the recommended
  tool to test and set up a gripper, with a gripper panel for the MSG and the SSG-48; see
  [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/motor-gui/). The earlier [SSG-gripper-GUI](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-gripper-GUI),
  a Python program, is legacy.
- **Python**: `pip install Spectral-BLDC`, the library the ROS 2 driver is built on; see
  [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/).
- **ROS 2**: the [msg_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2) package;
  see [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ros2/).
- **PAROL6 and PAR6**: the robots' own software drives the gripper; see [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/).
- **For a self-built gripper**: a 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter ([serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter))
  for the driver's UART port, to configure the driver with Motor GUI or a terminal; see
  [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/). For a self-build we recommend the
  [STEPFOC starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-starter-kit): it has this adapter and the rest of what the driver's setup needs
  ([Kits and the shop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/#kits-and-the-shop)).

## Optional

- **Jaws** for your objects: the printed jaws in the repository (solid, hollow, or with a TPU pad), sponge tape
  for the gripping faces, or your own design; see [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/).
- **A camera**: an OV9732 USB module for the camera mount; see [Variants](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/variants/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/02-safety/ -->

# Safety

The MSG gripper is a force-controlled gripper for collaborative and research robots, not a certified safety
component. Whoever puts it on a machine is responsible for the risk assessment of the gripper, the robot and
everything around them. Read this chapter before you power the gripper; the rules here are the ones that injure a
hand or destroy the gripper when they are ignored.

## Mechanical

!!! danger "The jaws"
    The jaws are a pinch point. With the current limit at the stepper's rating they close with tens of newtons,
    enough to crush a finger, and at full speed they travel the whole stroke in well under a second. Never put a
    finger between the jaws of a powered gripper. Keep hands away during calibration, which moves the jaws over
    the whole stroke without any command from you.

!!! warning "Start low"
    Test every new setup with a low current and speed: current 300 to 500 mA, speed 30. Raise them step by step
    once the application behaves, and never above the stepper's rated current
    ([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)).

!!! warning "Objects"
    A gripped object that slips, or that the jaws crush, can fly or fall. The grip force is a current limit, not a
    measurement: a hard object takes the full force, a soft one deforms until the force is reached.

### Clothing, hair and eyes

The jaws, and the open rack and pinion behind them, catch more than fingers: long hair, loose sleeves, gloves,
lanyards, rings and bracelets. Tie back long hair and take those off before you work at a powered gripper, and
keep them out of the jaws' travel while it calibrates or moves. Wear safety glasses when a gripped part can break,
slip or be thrown.

### If a finger is caught

!!! danger "The E-stop does not open the jaws"
    The gripper's E-stop bit and Send_ESTOP stop the jaws where they are; they do not open them, and a powered
    gripper holds its grip. To free a finger, switch off the gripper's supply: without current the stepper holds
    nothing beyond its own friction, and the jaws can be pushed apart by hand. A gripper without an error opens
    with a move to position 0 as well (**Open** in Motor GUI). Keep the supply's switch within reach while you
    test.

## Electrical

!!! danger "The cable"
    The gripper's M8 connector carries 24 V next to the CAN bus. A cable with the wrong pinout destroys the driver:
    the cable of the other Source Robotics robot reverses the supply, and a self-made one with a wrong pin can
    put 24 V on a CAN pin. Use the cable
    made for your robot or check every pin of your own; see [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/).

!!! warning "Supply"
    24 V DC. The driver inside tolerates 12 to 29 V, but the gripper's force and speed figures assume 24 V.

!!! warning "Do not unplug a powered gripper"
    Connect and disconnect the cable with the supply off. Hot-plugging the connector can damage the driver.

## Temperature

A thermistor on the motor housing measures the motor's temperature. At 75 °C the driver raises a temperature error and the gripper goes
idle; it clears when the motor has cooled and the error is cleared. A gripper holding an object at a high current
for long heats up: for a long hold, use the lowest current that holds the object. A self-built gripper without the
thermistor on its motor has no protection and can burn out its motor; see [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/).

## Stopping the gripper

- The E-stop bit of the move command (`Send_gripper_data_pack`) stops the gripper and raises the gripper E-stop
  error. The error stays as long as the last command carries the bit: send a command with the bit at 0, then
  clear it ([Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/)).
- `Send_ESTOP` to the driver, or `#Idle` over UART, stops it as well.
- The CAN watchdog ([Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/)) stops the gripper by itself when the host stops
  talking, which is the right protection for a program that may crash mid-grip.
- Cutting the supply releases the grip: a stepper without current holds nothing beyond its own friction, so an
  object can drop.

None of these is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop that cuts
the power, independent of the gripper and the robot software.

## Care

The gripper is not waterproof or dustproof: the rail and the racks are open to dust, chips and liquids. Keep it out
of wet or dusty places. What to check, and when to grease the mechanism, is in [Maintenance](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/07-maintenance/).

## Liability

The MSG gripper is sold as a component for people who build their own machines, and its designs are published
for people who build the gripper itself. The hardware designs, the firmware and this documentation are under
development and may contain errors. Whoever builds or operates
a machine with the gripper is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation. The
[full disclaimer](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/SAFETY_WARNING_AND_DISCLAIMER.md)
is in the product repository.


---

# Specifications

## Electrical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Supply voltage | 24 V DC; the driver tolerates 12 to 29 V, the force and speed figures assume 24 V |
| Idle power | 0.5 W |
| Motor current | up to 1.5 A (21.5 mm stepper), 2.0 A (40 mm), 2.1 A (60 mm); set per move as the grip force |
| Interface | CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers; node ID 0 as shipped |
| Connector | M8, 4 pins: 24 V, GND, CANH, CANL |
| CAN termination | 120 Ω, switchable, reachable through the stepper cover |
| Service port | the driver's UART, 3.3 V, 256000 baud, inside the housing |
| Driver | STEPFOC stepper controller, field-oriented control, 14-bit encoder on the motor shaft |
| Temperature protection | thermistor on the motor housing, 75 °C limit (changeable with `#Tlim`) |

## Mechanical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Stroke | 55 mm (100 mm rail), 105 mm (150 mm rail), 155 mm (200 mm rail) |
| Mass | about 380 g with the 150 mm rail and the 21.5 mm stepper; a longer rail or stepper adds to it; centre of mass and inertia on [Data for robot integration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/integration-data/) |
| Position resolution | 1/255 of the stroke: 0.2 to 0.6 mm per step of the position byte |
| Drive | NEMA 17 stepper, pinion (32 DP, 21 teeth, 8.3 mm pitch radius) on two racks, MGN7 linear rail |
| Grip force | ideal combined force up to about 31 N (21.5 mm stepper), 50 N (40 mm) or 76 N (60 mm) at the stepper's maximum current; see the model assumptions in [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Jaw speed | up to about 190 mm/s per jaw at speed 255; see [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Grasps | external (closing on the object) and internal (opening inside a hollow object) |
| Mounting | coupler plate for an 8 mm shaft (shaft coupler with M4 clamp screws); a ring cover for the PAROL6 wrist |
| Body material | PETG, printed with 25 % infill |
| Jaws | printed: solid, hollow, or a PETG body with a TPU pad; sponge tape on the faces |
| Camera | mount for an OV9732 USB camera module (100°), looking between the jaws |

## Environmental

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Operating temperature | −5 to 65 °C |
| Protection | none: not waterproof or dustproof |

## Variants

| Rail | Stroke | | Stepper | Motor | Maximum current | Assumed torque constant | Ideal combined force at the maximum current |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 mm | 55 mm | | 21.5 mm | 17HS08-1004S | 1.5 A | 0.17 Nm/A | about 31 N |
| 150 mm | 105 mm | | 40 mm | 17HS16-2004S1 | 2.0 A | 0.21 Nm/A | about 50 N |
| 200 mm | 155 mm | | 60 mm | 17HS24-2104S | 2.1 A | 0.30 Nm/A | about 76 N |

Any rail goes with any stepper, and the body comes in black or grey; see [Variants](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/variants/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/ -->

# Force and speed

A move command carries a current limit in mA and a speed from 0 to 255. This page estimates the resulting
force and speed. Force and payload values are ideal model estimates, not measured ratings.

## Grip force

The driver limits the motor's current to the value you command, so the torque the motor produces is limited to
$T = K_t \, I_q$, with $K_t$ the motor's torque constant in Nm/A (`#Kt` prints what the driver uses) and $I_q$
the current limit in amperes (the command is in mA). The pinion shares that torque between two racks.
Here $F$ is the **combined normal force of both jaws**,
not the force at one jaw:

$$
F = \frac{K_t \, I_q}{r}, \qquad r = 8.3\ \text{mm}
$$

$r$ is the pitch radius of the pinion (32 DP, 21 teeth). The force is proportional to the current, with a slope
set by the stepper:

| Stepper | Motor | Assumed $K_t$ | Ideal combined force per ampere | Maximum current | Ideal combined force at the maximum current |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm | 17HS08-1004S | 0.17 Nm/A | 20 N/A | 1.5 A | about 31 N |
| 40 mm | 17HS16-2004S1 | 0.21 Nm/A | 25 N/A | 2.0 A | about 50 N |
| 60 mm | 17HS24-2104S | 0.30 Nm/A | 36 N/A | 2.1 A | about 76 N |

![The grip force against the current limit for the three steppers, each up to its maximum current, from the formula above](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/grip_force_light.webp){ width="820" }
![The grip force against the current limit for the three steppers, each up to its maximum current, from the formula above](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/grip_force_dark.webp){ width="820" }

The curves use the listed torque constants; they are not force-gauge measurements. STEPFOC estimates `#Kt`
from a no-load speed/voltage test, rather than measuring shaft torque. The constant must match the driver's
$q$-axis current convention; a motor datasheet's current rating or supply current cannot be substituted directly.
A self-built gripper with another stepper needs its own force calibration. Below about
150 mA the motor does not move reliably, so the usable range starts at a few newtons. Motor GUI commands up to
1500 mA; the full force of the 40 mm and 60 mm steppers needs a command from Python or over CAN.

The current limit caps motor torque; it does not guarantee that the commanded current or the estimated
contact force is reached. Mechanism friction, finger flex and the contact position affect the actual force.

!!! danger "Stay within the stepper's maximum"
    The firmware clamps the gripper's current only at the driver's 2800 mA, above every stepper's maximum. A
    current above the stepper's maximum overheats the
    motor; the thermistor stops the gripper at 75 °C, but a motor driven far over its rating heats faster than
    the thermistor follows. The maximums are in the table above.

For a symmetric grip, each jaw applies $F/2$. The torque balance is
$T = F_\mathrm{left} r + F_\mathrm{right} r = F r$; counting $F$ once for each jaw would count the motor's torque twice.
These are theoretical forces before losses in the mechanism. A compression gauge between the jaws reads the
force at **one contact**; double that reading before comparing it with the combined force here. Record the
current, fingers and contact position when measuring; the same setup is needed for a useful comparison.

## Try it

<div class="gripper-calc" data-newtons-per-amp="25.3" data-radius-mm="8.3" data-ticks-min="500" data-ticks-max="60000" data-ticks-per-rev="16384" data-stroke-mm="105" markdown="0">
  <div class="gripper-calc__row gripper-calc__row--inline">
    <label for="gc-stepper">Stepper</label>
    <select id="gc-stepper" name="stepper">
      <option value="20.5" data-max-ma="1500">21.5 mm, 17HS08-1004S</option>
      <option value="25.3" data-max-ma="2000" selected>40 mm, 17HS16-2004S1</option>
      <option value="36.1" data-max-ma="2100">60 mm, 17HS24-2104S</option>
    </select>
    <label for="gc-rail">Rail</label>
    <select id="gc-rail" name="rail">
      <option value="55">100 mm, 55 mm stroke</option>
      <option value="105" selected>150 mm, 105 mm stroke</option>
      <option value="155">200 mm, 155 mm stroke</option>
    </select>
  </div>
  <div class="gripper-calc__row">
    <label for="gc-current">Current limit of the move: <output data-out="current">400 mA</output></label>
    <input id="gc-current" type="range" name="current" min="150" max="2000" step="10" value="400">
  </div>
  <div class="gripper-calc__row gripper-calc__row--inline">
    <label for="gc-mu">Friction coefficient µ</label>
    <input id="gc-mu" type="number" name="mu" min="0.1" max="1.5" step="0.05" value="0.3">
    <label for="gc-safety">Safety factor</label>
    <input id="gc-safety" type="number" name="safety" min="1" max="5" step="0.5" value="2">
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-calc__result">Ideal combined grip force <strong data-out="force">10 N</strong> · estimated static payload <strong data-out="payload">0.15 kg</strong> with the chosen friction and safety factor</p>
  <div class="gripper-calc__row">
    <label for="gc-speed">Speed byte: <output data-out="speedbyte">30</output></label>
    <input id="gc-speed" type="range" name="speed" min="0" max="255" step="1" value="30">
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-calc__result">Each jaw <strong data-out="jaw">24 mm/s</strong> · the jaws close at <strong data-out="closing">48 mm/s</strong> · the full stroke takes <strong data-out="stroke">2.2 s</strong></p>
</div>

The formulas of this page, with your numbers: the force from the current and the stepper's torque constant, the
weight held by friction with the safety factor of the next section, and the speed from the speed byte over the
rail's stroke.

## Payload

The grip force is not the weight the gripper can lift. An object held by friction between the two jaws is held
by $\mu(F_\mathrm{left} + F_\mathrm{right}) = \mu F$, with $\mu$ the friction coefficient between the jaw faces
and the object. Dividing the available friction force by a chosen safety factor $S$ gives the static estimate:

$$
W = \frac{\mu\,F}{S}, \qquad m = \frac{W}{g}
$$

Using an assumed $\mu$ = 0.3 and $S$ = 2, the model gives about 11 N of supported weight (1.2 kg) at 76 N
of combined grip force, or 4.7 N (0.47 kg) at 31 N. These are static estimates. Upward acceleration of 1 g
doubles the load; acceleration and emergency-stop loads need a separate check. Friction can be lower than
0.3, so measure it with your jaws on your object. A form-fit grip needs its own load assessment.

## Speed

The speed byte of a move is mapped by the firmware to the motor's speed in encoder ticks per second, linearly
from 500 at speed 0 to 60000 at speed 255:

$$
\text{ticks/s} = 500 + \frac{60000 - 500}{255}\, C
$$

The motor's encoder has 16384 ticks per revolution, so the angular speed is $\omega = \text{ticks/s} / 16384 \times 2\pi$
and each jaw moves at

$$
v = \omega \, r
$$

| Speed byte | Motor speed | Each jaw moves at | The jaws close at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 500 ticks/s, 0.03 rev/s | 1.6 mm/s | 3 mm/s |
| 30 | 7500 ticks/s, 0.46 rev/s | 24 mm/s | 48 mm/s |
| 128 | 30400 ticks/s, 1.9 rev/s | 97 mm/s | 190 mm/s |
| 255 | 60000 ticks/s, 3.7 rev/s | 190 mm/s | 380 mm/s |

Both jaws move, so the gap closes at twice the speed of one jaw. At speed 255 a 105 mm stroke takes about
0.3 s. The gripper calibration runs at speed 40 and 500 mA.

## Position

The position byte is linear over the stroke: 0 is the fully open end stop found by the gripper calibration, 255
the fully closed one. One step of the byte is the stroke divided by 255: 0.22 mm on the 100 mm rail, 0.41 mm on
the 150 mm rail, 0.61 mm on the 200 mm rail. The driver considers the position reached within 5 encoder ticks,
about 0.03 mm.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/connector/ -->

# Connector and pinout

The gripper has one connector, an M8 4-pin male on the side of the body, and one cable: 24 V and the CAN bus.

![The M8 connector on the gripper body and its four signals: 24V, GND, CANH, CANL](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_pinout.webp){ width="900" }

## Pin numbers

![M8 male on the gripper: front mating face and numbered signals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/m8-gripper-pinout.svg){ width="650" }

The drawing shows the connector's staggered contact layout. Look **into the male connector on
the gripper**, with its pins visible. The female cable connector has the
mirrored contact view. The solder side is also mirrored: use the numbers moulded into the connector, rather
than matching wire colours or the installed housing's rotation.

| Gripper pin | Signal | Connection |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **+24 V** | positive motor supply |
| **2** | **CANL** | CAN low |
| **3** | **GND** | power-supply return |
| **4** | **CANH** | CAN high, 1 Mbit/s with CANL |

These are the pin numbers the gripper is built with. The MSG and the SSG-48 share this wiring and
their cables; page 17 of the [SSG-48 assembly manual](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Gripper_assembly_manual.pdf) gives it,
in a photo of the connector from the back, where the wires are soldered: the mirror image of the picture above.
They describe the **gripper end**. PAROL6 and PAR6 use different connections at the robot end:
[The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/) gives both diagrams. Check continuity with the supply disconnected.

!!! danger "The wrong cable destroys the driver"
    A reversed supply or 24 V on a CAN pin destroys the driver inside the gripper the moment it is powered; the
    other robot's cable reverses the supply. Use the cable
    made for your robot; check a self-made cable pin by pin against the pin table above and the wiring diagram
    before you plug it in.

## Inside the housing

The STEPFOC driver's own connectors are inside: its UART port (3.3 V, JST SH, 4 pins) under the coupler plate,
used to configure a self-built gripper ([Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/uart/)), and its CAN termination switch,
reachable through an opening in the stepper cover ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)). The
driver's pinout is in the [STEPFOC documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/03-technical-data/connectors/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/dimensions/ -->

# Dimensions and CAD

<div class="gripper-viewer" data-base="../../assets/models/msg/" markdown="0">
  <canvas class="gripper-viewer__canvas" aria-label="The MSG gripper in 3D: drag to turn, scroll to zoom"></canvas>
  <div class="gripper-viewer__controls">
    <label class="gripper-viewer__field">Opening <input type="range" name="opening" min="0" max="100" value="50"></label>
    <label class="gripper-viewer__field">Body <span class="gripper-viewer__swatches" data-target="body"></span><input type="color" name="body" value="#d2d2cf" title="Any colour"></label>
    <label class="gripper-viewer__field">Jaws <span class="gripper-viewer__swatches" data-target="jaws"></span><input type="color" name="jaws_color" value="#1a1a1a" title="Any colour"></label>
    <button type="button" name="reset" class="md-button">Reset view</button>
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-viewer__hint">Drag to turn the gripper, scroll to zoom, open and close the jaws, try the colours. The model is the
gripper's URDF, the 150 mm rail with the 21.5 mm stepper; the current URDF and MuJoCo models are linked from the repository's <a href="https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/msg_description">msg_description</a> guide. The shop sells the body in black and grey.</p>
</div>

The drawings show the variant of the 3D model: the 150 mm rail, the 21.5 mm stepper and the solid jaws, with the
jaws fully open. All dimensions are in millimetres, measured on the gripper's CAD as the
[robot model](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/integration-data/) carries it. Heights are counted from the coupler's back face, the face that
rests against the robot; the coupler axis is the gripper's axis on the robot.

![Front view, from the camera side, jaws fully open: 159.40 mm over the jaw blockers at the ends of the rail, 153.00 mm over the jaws, 106.20 mm between the faces of the solid jaws, 110.30 mm from the coupler's back face to the jaw tips, which reach 74.30 mm beyond the rail block](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_front.webp){ width="900" }
![Front view, from the camera side, jaws fully open: 159.40 mm over the jaw blockers at the ends of the rail, 153.00 mm over the jaws, 106.20 mm between the faces of the solid jaws, 110.30 mm from the coupler's back face to the jaw tips, which reach 74.30 mm beyond the rail block](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_front_dark.webp){ width="900" }

![Side view: 116.32 mm from the jaws to the top of the camera mount, the jaws' centre line 28.35 mm from the coupler axis, an 8.50 mm thick coupler ring, the camera mount 59.65 mm in front of the coupler's back face, and the camera looking 50.00° off the coupler axis toward the jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_side.webp){ width="700" }
![Side view: 116.32 mm from the jaws to the top of the camera mount, the jaws' centre line 28.35 mm from the coupler axis, an 8.50 mm thick coupler ring, the camera mount 59.65 mm in front of the coupler's back face, and the camera looking 50.00° off the coupler axis toward the jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_side_dark.webp){ width="700" }

![Top view, from the jaw tips: 159.40 mm across, 116.32 mm from the jaws to the top of the camera mount, each jaw 24.40 by 25.40 mm at its carrier](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_top.webp){ width="900" }
![Top view, from the jaw tips: 159.40 mm across, 116.32 mm from the jaws to the top of the camera mount, each jaw 24.40 by 25.40 mm at its carrier](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_top_dark.webp){ width="900" }

![The coupler, seen from the robot: a ring of 54.10 mm diameter with a recess of 32.10 mm, round the coupler axis; the jaws' centre line 28.35 mm to one side of the axis, the top of the camera mount 78.97 mm to the other](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_coupler.webp){ width="900" }
![The coupler, seen from the robot: a ring of 54.10 mm diameter with a recess of 32.10 mm, round the coupler axis; the jaws' centre line 28.35 mm to one side of the axis, the top of the camera mount 78.97 mm to the other](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/dimensions/msg_coupler_dark.webp){ width="900" }

The recess is 6.50 mm deep; the flange of the shaft coupler sits in it. The PAROL6 ring cover has the same 54.10
and 32.10 mm circles ([Mounting on a robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/mounting/)). `tools/dimension_drawings.py` in this site's
repository draws the four views from the model and prints every number on them.

## Other rails and steppers

The rail sets the width and the stroke; the stepper sets how far the stepper cover, and the camera mount on top of
it, stand away from the rail. Neither changes the coupler, the jaws or the 110.30 mm to the jaw tips. The lengths
below are measured in the parts' STEP files; the overall sizes add them to the drawn variant.

| Rail | Stroke | Body | Over the jaw blockers | Printed parts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 mm | 55 mm | 103.00 mm | 109.40 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_100mm`, `gripper_jaw_100mm_L/R` |
| 150 mm (drawn) | 105 mm | 153.00 mm | 159.40 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_150mm`, `gripper_jaw_150mm_L/R` |
| 200 mm | 155 mm | 203.00 mm | 209.40 mm | `MSG_Gripper_body_200mm`, `gripper_jaw_200mm_L/R` |

The jaw blockers at the two ends of the rail are 3.20 mm thick each. On the drawn 150 mm rail the open jaws stand
flush with the ends of the body (153.00 mm over the jaws).

| Stepper | Motor | Stepper cover | Cover's outer end, from the 21.5 mm one | Jaws to the top of the camera mount | Coupler axis to the top of the camera mount |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm (drawn) | 17HS08-1004S | 34.40 mm | 0 | 116.32 mm | 78.97 mm |
| 40 mm | 17HS16-2004S1 | 51.40 mm | +18.50 mm | 134.82 mm | 97.47 mm |
| 60 mm | 17HS24-2104S | 71.40 mm | +38.50 mm | 154.82 mm | 117.47 mm |

## CAD

The STEP files of every part are in the product repository, and are the reference for anything that has to fit:

- [STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files):
  `Common parts` (the ring covers, the camera mount and its lid, the connector lid, the jaw blocker, the stepper
  spacer), `Linear rail dependant parts` (the body and the jaw carriers per rail length), `Stepper dependant parts`
  (the covers and spacers per stepper length), `Gripper jaws attachment` (the jaw designs), `Tools` (the magnet
  tool). There is no STEP file of the whole gripper; the robot model below is the assembled gripper.
- [Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files):
  the same parts as 3MF, ready to slice.

![The STEP model of the gripper without its jaws, seen from the front, into the camera](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_3D_model.webp){ width="600" }

## For simulation

The product repository's [msg_description](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/msg_description)
guide links the gripper's models, which are kept in [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions):
standalone URDF and MJCF (MuJoCo) packages of the gripper with solid or soft TPU jaws, with their meshes, collision
shapes and mass properties, and the PAROL6 and PAR6 models with the gripper mounted. The numbers a robot needs,
the tool centre point, the mass and the inertia, are on [Data for robot integration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/integration-data/).

[CAD and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/cad-files/) lists everything that can be downloaded.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/integration-data/ -->

# Data for robot integration

What a robot's software needs to carry the gripper: the frame the numbers are given in, the mass, the centre of
mass and the inertia, and the tool centre point (TCP). The numbers are taken from the gripper's robot model in
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions) (version 2.18.1, `msg_description`
in URDF and `msg` in MJCF) and moved into the frame below. The model is the 150 mm rail with the 21.5 mm stepper,
the variant of the [drawings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/dimensions/).

## The frame

The origin is on the coupler axis, at the centre of the coupler's back face: the face that rests against the
robot.

- **Z** runs along the coupler axis, from the robot toward the jaw tips: the approach direction.
- **Y** runs along the jaw travel, parallel to the rail, positive toward the side of the M8 connector.
- **X** completes the frame: from the rail and the jaws toward the stepper and the camera. The jaws' centre line
  is at X = −28.35 mm, the top of the camera mount at X = +78.97 mm.

The axes are those of the model's `flange` frame. That frame's origin lies 15.50 mm further along Z, inside the
body behind the coupler ring: subtract 15.50 mm from a Z below to have it in the model's `flange` frame.

## Mass and inertia

| Model, jaws | Mass measured | Mass in the model | Centre of mass x, y, z (mm) | Ixx, Iyy, Izz (10⁻⁶ kg·m²) | Ixy, Ixz, Iyz (10⁻⁶ kg·m²) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| URDF, jaws open | about 380 g | 380.0 g | −0.70, 0.22, 32.34 | 508.5, 147.6, 525.5 | 0.4, 42.0, −1.9 |
| URDF, jaws closed | about 380 g | 380.0 g | −0.70, 0.22, 32.34 | 200.2, 147.6, 217.2 | 0.4, 42.0, 0.2 |
| MJCF, jaws open | about 380 g | 380.0 g | −0.42, 0.24, 31.89 | 471.7, 137.5, 488.0 | 0.6, 35.7, −5.7 |
| MJCF, jaws closed | about 380 g | 380.0 g | −0.42, 0.24, 31.89 | 199.6, 137.5, 215.9 | 0.5, 35.7, 1.6 |

The model's mass is the body, 301.4 g, and two moving assemblies of 39.3 g each (the rail carriage, the jaw
carrier and the jaw). The inertia is about the centre of mass, with the axes of the frame above, as the elements of
the inertia tensor that a URDF's `<inertia>` takes. The solid and the soft TPU jaws have the same mass data in the
model, so one row serves both. Closed is the model's closed end of the travel. Opening and closing move the two
jaws along Y by the same amount in opposite directions: the centre of mass stays where it is, Ixx and Izz change.
The URDF and the MJCF model give the jaws different centres of mass and inertias, hence the two pairs of rows.

## Tool centre point

| Jaws | The point | x (mm) | y (mm) | z (mm) | Orientation | Opening |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solid | the middle between the jaw tips | −28.35 | 0 | 110.30 | the frame's axes | any |
| Solid | the middle between the gripping faces | −28.43 | 0 | 79.65 | the frame's axes | any |
| Soft TPU | the middle between the jaw tips | −28.35 | 0 | 110.30 | the frame's axes | any |
| Soft TPU | the middle between the TPU pads | −28.43 | 0 | 80.15 | the frame's axes | any |
| Both | the model's `tcp` frame | −28.35 | 0 | 99.30 | the frame's axes | any |

The two jaws move by the same amount in opposite directions, so each point stays on the gripper's centre plane
(y = 0) at every opening. A gripping face is the centre of its area: the solid jaw's face is 18.00 mm wide along X
and runs from z = 51.30 to 110.30 mm, the TPU pad from z = 52.30 to 110.30 mm. Fully open, the solid jaws' faces
are 106.20 mm apart, the TPU pads 104.20 mm. The model's `tcp` is its control point on the jaws' centre line,
11.00 mm short of the tips, the same for both jaws; robot_descriptions says it is not a measured grasp centre.

## How accurate this is

The masses are measured: about 380 g for the whole gripper with the 150 mm rail and the 21.5 mm stepper (the
variant the model shows), 39.3 g for each moving assembly (an approximate
figure). The centres of mass and the inertias are not: robot_descriptions 2.18.1 calls them existing, unverified
estimates, not scaled to the measured masses or checked against the CAD's mass distribution. Use them for
simulation and for a first payload setting, not as a measurement. The model has one variant; a longer rail or
stepper is heavier and moves the centre of mass toward the extra part, and the model does not say by how much.

## Where the numbers go

In the PAROL6 Python API the MSG is a built-in tool, `rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")`, with its TCP at
(−29, 0, −109.5) mm in the API's flange frame, whose Z points back into the wrist
([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/latest/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/));
in a URDF, the mass, the centre of mass and the inertia go into the gripper link's `<inertial>` and the TCP into a
fixed joint from the mounting frame.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/ -->

# Installation

Putting the gripper on a robot: the mounting, the cable that carries its power and its CAN bus, the jaws for
your objects, and the CAN termination.

## In this chapter

- [Mounting on a robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/mounting/)
- [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/)
- [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/)
- [CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)

When all of it is done, continue with [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/mounting/ -->

# Mounting on a robot

The gripper mounts by its coupler plate, the round plate on the back of the body behind the stepper. Two covers
exist for it, and the STEP files let you make a third.

## An 8 mm shaft

As shipped, the coupler plate carries a shaft coupler with an 8 mm bore and M4 clamp screws under the `ring_cover`
part: the gripper slides onto an 8 mm shaft and is clamped with the two M4 screws. Any robot or fixture that
offers an 8 mm shaft takes the gripper this way.

![The coupler plate with the 8 mm shaft coupler](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_conn_8mm.webp){ width="600" }

## PAROL6

For the PAROL6 wrist, replace `ring_cover` with `ring_cover-PAROL6` from the STEP files (`Common parts`): it bolts
to the robot's last joint. Tighten the shaft coupler's two clamp screws with blue threadlocker. The PAROL6
gripper cable then runs from the gripper to the robot's gripper port; see [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/) and
[On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/), which also has the joint 5 homing offset.

![The gripper with the PAROL6 ring cover (red)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/MSG_with_parol_cover.webp){ width="600" }

## Another robot

Adapt `ring_cover`, or the body itself, to your flange: the STEP files are open. Keep the gripper's connector
reachable and the camera's view free, and route the cable so that it cannot be pulled by the robot's motion.

## On the bench

For testing, clamp the body, not the jaws or the rail, and leave the whole stroke free: calibration moves the
jaws from one end stop to the other without any command from you.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/ -->

# The cable

![PAROL6 and PAR6 gripper cables are not interchangeable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/cable_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

One cable with an M8 4-pin connector powers the gripper and carries its CAN bus. The robot end differs from robot
to robot.

!!! danger "PAROL6 and PAR6 cables are different"
    The two robots put the four signals on different pins of their gripper port. The PAROL6 cable in a PAR6, or
    the other way round, reverses the gripper's supply, 24 V on its GND pin, and destroys its driver. Use the cable sold for your
    robot, and check a self-made cable pin by pin.

## The cables from the shop

| Robot | Cable |
|---|---|
| PAROL6 | [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) |
| PAR6 | the PAR6 gripper cable, coming to the shop |

## Making your own

For a bench setup, another robot, or a replacement, the cable is four wires between an M8 4-pin female connector
at the gripper and whatever the other end needs:

| Part | Quantity | BOM |
|---|---|---|
| 26 AWG 4-wire twisted-pair cable, 0.15 mm², shielded | about 0.4 m | [cable](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c4m3ggwn) |
| M8 4-pin female cable connector (the gripper has the male) | 1 | [connector](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c4OWHPKF) |
| M8 4-pin male cable connector, for a robot with an M8 port | 1 | the same listing |

<div class="grid" markdown>
![The M8 male connector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/M8_male.webp){ width="260" }
![The M8 female connector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/M8_female.webp){ width="260" }
![A finished cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/cable_assembly.webp){ width="340" }
</div>

Wire it as the diagram for your robot shows. Pin 1 to 4 are the numbers moulded into the M8 connectors; the
colours are those of the cable in the BOM.

=== "PAROL6"
    ![The PAROL6 cable: the pins are crossed between the two ends](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/PAROL6_cable.webp){ width="320" }

    Male end at the robot, female end at the gripper: pin 1 to 3, 2 to 4, 3 to 1, 4 to 2. The PAROL6 socket has
    GND on pin 1, CANH on 2, 24 V on 3 and CANL on 4; the cable brings each signal to the gripper's pin for it.

=== "PAR6"
    ![The PAR6 cable: pin to pin](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/PAR6_cable.png){ width="200" }

=== "Bench or your own robot"
    Connect the gripper's 24V and GND to a 24 V supply and its CANH and CANL to your CAN interface; on a PC that
    is the CANvas adapter's CAN terminals. [Connector and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/connector/) shows which
    pin of the gripper's connector is which signal. Twist the CAN pair, keep the cable short at 1 Mbit/s, and
    terminate the bus at both ends ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)).

Connect the shield at one end only. Check continuity and the absence of shorts between all four pins before the
first power-up.

## Handling

Plug and unplug with the supply off. Route the cable along the robot with enough slack for the wrist's full
motion, and keep it away from the jaws' travel.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/ -->

# Jaws

The jaws bolt to the two carriers on the rail and are yours to adapt. The product repository has three designs,
all in [Gripper jaws attachment](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Gripper%20jaws%20attachment);
each file is one jaw, mirrored in the slicer for the other side, except the solid jaw, which has a mirrored file.

| Design | File | Use |
|---|---|---|
| PETG body with a glued-on TPU pad | `MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE` | the recommended jaw: the soft pad deforms around the object and holds it better |
| Solid jaw | `MSG_solid_jaw`, `MSG_solid_jaw_mirror` | one part, quick to print |
| Hollow jaw | `MSG_JAW_HOLLOW` | lighter, and suited to multi-colour prints |

![The jaw body, with the mounting holes for the carrier](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/gripper_jaws.webp){ width="520" }

## The TPU jaw

![The TPU jaw: a PETG body (black) and a TPU pad (yellow)](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/tpujaws.webp){ width="700" }

Print the body in PETG with your usual settings and the pad in TPU with 16 % infill, no top or bottom layers and
two walls, for the softest pad. Then glue the pad to the body with ordinary super glue, in the orientation the
pictures show: a pad glued the wrong way round leaves the jaws facing the wrong direction.

<div class="grid" markdown>
![Apply super glue](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/jaw_glue.webp){ width="300" }
![Press the pad on](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/jaw_assembly.webp){ width="300" }
![Check the orientation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/jaw_orientation.webp){ width="300" }
</div>

## Sponge pads

A strip of 1 mm sponge tape (30 mm wide, in the BOM) on the gripping face of any jaw improves the hold on hard
and smooth objects a great deal. Cut it to length, peel the backing and press it on.

## Your own jaws

Keep the carrier's hole pattern from one of the designs and shape the rest for your objects. Long jaws
multiply the lever arm on the carriers: keep them short and stiff, and remember that the grip force is set at the
jaw faces, not at the rail.

!!! warning "Custom jaws on a PAR6"
    On a PAR6, custom jaws must keep the size of the original jaws: no longer, no wider and no thicker. The
    PAR6 software works with the gripper's original dimensions (its collision model of the tool and the tool
    centre point), so a larger jaw reaches where the robot does not expect it.

## Calibrate after changing the jaws

The gripper calibration finds the end stops with the jaws fitted; jaws that meet earlier or later than the old
ones change where 255 is. Calibrate again after a change, which happens at the next power-up anyway.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/ -->

# CAN termination

A CAN bus needs a 120 Ω resistor at each of its two ends. The gripper's driver has one, on a switch that is
reachable through an opening in the stepper cover: slide it to the **ON** mark to connect the resistor, away from
it to disconnect it.

![The termination switch of the driver, seen through the stepper cover](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/Gripper_termination.jpg){ width="700" }

| The gripper is | Switch |
|---|---|
| the last node on a robot's bus, at the end of the arm | ON |
| alone on a bench bus with the CANvas adapter (which has its own termination) | ON |
| in the middle of a bus, with other nodes after it | off |

A bus with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CANH and CANL with everything unpowered. A missing
or doubled termination shows up as lost frames and a gripper that answers only sometimes.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/ -->

# First setup

For the complete bench procedure, use the [one-page quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/quick-start/).

From a mounted and cabled gripper to one that opens and closes on command. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual
tool for it; every step also gives the Python call and the UART command.

1. [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/motor-gui/): the browser, the CANvas adapter, connecting to the gripper, the gripper panel.
2. [Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/first-moves/): the three things every session starts with, and the first grip.

A self-built gripper first needs its driver set up, which a bought one already has: [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/)
in the build guide.

A gripper that has been through these pages is ready for [Operation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/motor-gui/ -->

# Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) is Source Robotics' tool for its drivers and for the grippers built on them: a
page in the browser that reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access, so there is nothing to
install. With the CANvas adapter on the gripper's CAN bus it calibrates and activates the gripper, opens and closes
it, shows its state and plots its position and current. It is the recommended tool for the first setup and for
testing; everything it does is one CAN message, so what you learn here carries over to
[Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/) and the other interfaces.

!!! note "The gripper GUI is legacy"
    The earlier [SSG-gripper-GUI](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-gripper-GUI), a Python program with a
    Windows build, still works with both grippers but is not developed further. Use Motor GUI.

## What you need

- A Chromium-based browser: Chrome, Edge, Brave or Opera. The serial port access Motor GUI relies on (Web Serial)
  is not in Firefox or Safari.
- The [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) in a USB port and on the
  gripper's CAN bus, with the bus terminated ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)), and the
  gripper powered.
- Nothing on the gripper itself: a bought gripper is ready. The browser's port access and the adapter's
  installation are described on the STEPFOC site, [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/05-setup/motor-gui/).

## Connecting

1. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/). In the connection bar choose **CAN (slcan)** and the bitrate
   1 Mbit/s, then connect: the browser asks which serial port, pick the CANvas adapter.
2. Choose the gripper's node in the node picker: its CAN ID, 0 unless you changed it. Switch the bar from
   **Motor** to **Gripper**.
3. The gripper panel fills in as soon as the gripper's feedback arrives: calibrated or not, activated or not, the
   position, the current and the errors. While it says that it is waiting for feedback, check the node ID, the
   power and that the driver is in gripper mode.

The panel works with one gripper at a time; to work with another on the same bus, pick its node. The **Motor**
side of the switch shows the same driver as a motor, which the gripper does not need.

!!! success "Check"
    The gripper panel shows the gripper's position and current, and *Not calibrated* after a power-up. If the
    browser's port list does not show the adapter, see the notes for your system below; if the panel keeps
    waiting for feedback, step 3 and [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/).

### The adapter's port on your system

=== "Windows"
    The CANvas adapter appears in Device Manager under **Ports (COM & LPT)** as a COM port, and the browser's
    port list shows it. Close any other program that holds the port, a Python script or another browser tab:
    the connection fails at once while it is open elsewhere.

=== "Linux"
    The browser opens the port only if your user may. Add yourself to the `dialout` group once, then log out and
    in again:

    ```
    sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
    ```

=== "macOS"
    Nothing to install. A browser installed with Homebrew or from the App Store may need USB access: Motor GUI's
    own guide points to System Settings, **Privacy & Security**.

## Try it without a gripper

Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)** and **Connect**, then switch to **Gripper**.
The whole panel runs in the browser without an adapter or a gripper. The mock device identifies itself as
SSG-48; MSG uses the same controls.

## The gripper panel

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">

![Calibrated and activated gripper demo with command controls and plots](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/motor-gui/gripper-ready-demo.jpg){ width="1000" }

<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:17%" aria-hidden="true">1</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:54%" aria-hidden="true">2</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:88%;top:17%" aria-hidden="true">3</span>

</div>
<figcaption markdown="1">**1. State:** calibrated, activated, and no errors. **2. Commands:** position, speed and current, each applied with its Set button. **3. Plots:** position and current feedback. Captured from the **SSG-48 mock demo**; MSG uses the same controls.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Calibrate** | runs the gripper calibration: the jaws travel the whole stroke to find the end stops. The panel asks you to confirm; clear any error, deactivate the gripper and take everything out of the jaws first. Press nothing else until the panel says *Calibrated*: a move or **Clear errors** during the calibration ends it |
| **Activate**, **Deactivate** | the activate bit: a calibrated gripper carries out moves only while it is activated |
| *Position*, *Speed*, *Current*, each with **Set** | the move: position 0 (open) to 255 (closed), speed 0 to 255, current limit 0 to 1500 mA, which is the force. Each **Set** sends its value together with the other two as last sent |
| **Open**, **Close** | a move to position 0 or 255 with the set speed and current |
| **Stop** | ends the move where the jaws are |
| **E-stop**, or ++esc++ | stops the gripper at once: the move command with the E-stop bit, after which the gripper reports the E-stop error until a command with the bit at 0 has been sent and the error cleared |
| **Clear errors** | clears the errors; an error whose cause remains comes straight back |
| Plots | position and current, live, with the requested position drawn in; the window and the scale are adjustable, and **Export CSV** saves a recorded run |
| Events | the feedback rate and the recent gripper events, with **Export events** for diagnostics |
| Cycle test | moves between two positions at a speed and a current, a number of times with a dwell: for endurance tests and demonstrations. Keep the tab visible while it runs |

Motor GUI's current limit stops at 1500 mA. The 40 mm and 60 mm steppers take more
([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)); for their full force, command the move from
Python or over CAN.

## Presets for a self-built gripper

Connected over **UART** instead, through the [serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter)
on the driver's UART port, Motor GUI's setup page has tuned presets for the grippers: *MSG 21.5 mm motor*, *MSG 40 mm
motor* and *MSG 60 mm motor*, and *SSG-48* for the other gripper. A preset writes the
motor's parameters, the loop gains, gripper mode, the thermistor and the CAN ID to the driver and saves them; its
CAN ID is 6, the PAR6 gripper's, so change it before applying for another robot.
[Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/) says when to apply it, and lists the same settings as commands
for a terminal.
