## What next

[Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/first-moves/) is the first session with a connected gripper.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/05-setup/first-moves/ -->

# Calibrate, activate, move

Every session with the gripper starts the same way: clear what errors there are, calibrate, activate. Then it
moves. This page does it once with Motor GUI, with Python and over UART; [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/)
explains what happens inside.

!!! danger
    The jaws move over the whole stroke during calibration, and close with the set force afterwards. Nothing in
    reach of them, fingers included.

## 1. Power up

At power-up the gripper reports *Not calibrated* and does not move. Its stepper must be calibrated too, which a
bought gripper is from the factory; a self-built gripper gets that in [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/).

## 2. Clear errors

The driver powers up in an error state until its motor is calibrated and it has run through its checks; an
E-stop, an over-temperature or a supply fault leave an error too. A gripper with an error does not move, and
does not calibrate either: clear first.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Clear errors**, when the panel shows an error.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_Clear_Error()
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Clear
    ```

An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; after an E-stop, send a command with the E-stop bit
at 0 before you clear. [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/) says what each needs.

!!! success "Check"
    Motor GUI shows no error; in Python the three error attributes read 0 after the next status poll; over UART,
    `#Error` prints `No errors!`. An error that is back at once still has its cause:
    [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/).

## 3. Calibrate

The gripper calibration finds the two end stops: the jaws open fully, pause, then close fully, at low force
(500 mA) and low speed. Each end is recognised when the jaws have stood still against it for half a second. It
takes about ten seconds; the result is not kept over a power cycle, so this runs at every power-up.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Calibrate**, and confirm. When the jaws stop, the panel shows *Calibrated*; press nothing else until then.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()
    time.sleep(10)       # send nothing meanwhile; With Python waits for the calibrated bit instead
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Gripcal
    ```

If the jaws do not move at all, or move to one end and stop: the gripper is in an error state (clear it first, see
step 2), or the stepper is not calibrated. If the routine runs for 24 seconds and gives up, an end stop was not
found: something blocks the jaws short of the end, or the mechanism is too stiff for 500 mA.

Until the gripper reports *Calibrated*, send nothing but status polls: a move command or a clear during the
calibration ends it, and the gripper stays uncalibrated.

!!! success "Check"
    The jaws opened fully, then closed fully, and the gripper reports *Calibrated*: in Motor GUI's panel, as
    `gripper_calibrated` = 1 in Python, or `Gripper calibrated is: 1` from `#Gripinfo`. If not after 24 s:
    [Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/#calibration).

## 4. Activate

A calibrated gripper carries out a move only while it is activated.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Activate**. The panel shows *Activated*.

=== "Python"
    The activate bit is part of every move command, its fourth argument; send it as 1. To activate without
    moving, send a command with the action bit, the fifth argument, at 0:

    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(0, 30, 300, 1, 0, 0, 0)   # position, speed, current, activate = 1, action = 0, E-stop, release direction
    ```

=== "UART"
    `#Grippos` activates by itself; `#Gripact 1` activates without moving.

!!! success "Check"
    The panel shows *Activated*; in Python `gripper_activated` reads 1; `#Gripinfo` prints
    `Gripper activated is: 1`.

## 5. Move

A move is three numbers: the position (0 open, 255 closed), the speed (0 to 255: linear from 1.6 to 190 mm/s at
each jaw) and the current limit in mA, which is the grip force ([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)).
Start with speed 30, about 24 mm/s at each jaw, and 300 mA.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Set *Speed* 30 and *Current* 300 with their **Set** buttons, then **Close** and **Open**, or set a *Position*:
    the jaws follow, the plots show the position and the current, and the state says whether the jaws reached
    the position or stopped on something.

=== "Python"
    ```python
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(200, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)   # position, speed, current, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
    time.sleep(2)
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    ```

=== "UART"
    ```
    #Gripvel 30
    #Gripcur 300
    #Grippos 200
    #Grippos 20
    ```

Put an object between the jaws and close on it: the jaws stop on it and hold it with 300 mA, and the state reads
*object detected while closing*. Raise the current for a firmer grip, within the stepper's rating, and the speed
once the motion is what you want.

!!! success "Check"
    The jaws go to each position and the state reads *at position*; on the object they stop and the state reads
    *object detected while closing*. If they do not move:
    [It does not move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/#it-does-not-move).

## What the gripper reports

Every move command is answered with the gripper's state, which Motor GUI shows in its panel and the
library puts into attributes: the position, the current, whether it is calibrated and activated, whether a move
is in progress, the object-detection result, and the three error bits. [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/)
goes through them.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ -->

# Operation

How a working gripper is used: what happens inside when it calibrates and moves, the interfaces it is driven
through, and what to do when it reports an error.

## In this chapter

- [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/)
- [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/can/)
- [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/uart/)
- [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/)
- [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ros2/)
- [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/)
- [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/)

The exact layout of every message and command is in the [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/ -->

# How the gripper works

The gripper is a state machine in the driver's firmware, fed by one command and answering with one status. This
page is what it does with them.

## The states

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up
    NotCalibrated --> Calibrating: Send_gripper_calibrate / #Gripcal
    Calibrating --> Calibrated: both end stops found
    Calibrating --> NotCalibrated: not done in 24 s, or a full command or a clear
    Calibrated --> Moving: command with activate = 1, action = 1
    Moving --> Holding: object found, or position reached
    Holding --> Moving: a different command
    Moving --> Stopped: action = 0 or activate = 0
    Holding --> Stopped: action = 0 or activate = 0
    Stopped --> Moving: command with action = 1
    Moving --> Idle: error, E-stop, clear
    Holding --> Idle: error, E-stop, clear
    Idle --> Moving: errors cleared, then a command
```

**Not calibrated**

- After power-up the gripper does not know where its jaws are.
- It answers status requests and refuses moves.
- The gripper calibration is not kept over a power cycle.

**Calibrating**

- The jaws open at speed 40 and 500 mA until they have stood still against the end stop for half a second.
- They pause briefly, then close the same way.
- The two end positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed).
- If the whole routine has not found both end stops within 24 seconds of its start, it gives up and the
  gripper stays uncalibrated.
- While it runs, send only empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames, the status poll. A full gripper command or
  Send_Clear_Error ends the calibration where it is, and the gripper stays uncalibrated.
- Send_gripper_calibrate has no answer; the calibrated bit of the status turns 1 when the routine is done.

**Moving**

- A command with the activate and action bits set starts a move towards the position, at the speed.
- The current is limited to the commanded value.
- The driver runs its velocity loop towards the target and watches two things: the speed of the jaws and the
  motor current.

**Holding**: the move ends in one of two ways.

- **Position reached** (within 5 encoder ticks): the driver switches to position control and holds the jaws
  there. Object detection reads 3.
- **Object in the way**: the jaws stop before the target with the current at its limit. The driver keeps pushing
  with the limited current, which is the grip. Object detection reads 1 if the jaws were closing, 2 if they were
  opening.
- Either way, nothing moves until a different command arrives.

**Stopped**

- A command with the action bit at 0, or with the activate bit at 0, stops the move.
- The driver keeps the jaws still: it runs its velocity loop at zero speed with the command's current limit, so
  the jaws resist being moved, and the object detection keeps reporting.
- The next command with the activate and action bits set moves the jaws again.

**Idle**

- An error, the E-stop bit, Send_Clear_Error, Send_Idle or `#Idle` takes the gripper to idle.
- The motor is no longer driven and holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction, so an object can slip.
- After an error, clear it; then the next command with the action bit set moves the gripper again.

## The command

Send_gripper_data_pack carries, in 5 bytes:

| Field | Range | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Position | 0 to 255 | 0 fully open, 255 fully closed, linear over the stroke |
| Speed | 0 to 255 | 1.6 to 190 mm/s at each jaw, linear (500 to 60000 encoder ticks per second); see [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Current | mA | the current limit of the move, so the grip force; clamped by the firmware only at 2800 mA |
| Activate | bit | 1 activates the gripper; 0 deactivates it: the move stops and the jaws are held still |
| Action | bit | 1 carries out the move; 0 stores the command and holds the jaws still where they are |
| E-stop | bit | 1 stops the gripper and raises the E-stop error, again at every cycle while the bit stays 1 |
| Release direction | bit | read by the firmware but not used |

The same command sent twice does nothing new: the driver compares every command with the previous one, and only
a changed command resets the "at position" state and starts a move. So a host may repeat the command at any
rate, which the CAN watchdog needs; to move the jaws from a held position to the same position again, change
the speed or the current by one.

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack, 0 bytes, changes nothing and is answered like a full one: it is the status poll,
and it costs the bus almost nothing. A host usually sends one full command per move and polls with empty ones.

Over UART, `#Grippos` is the same command: it sets the position, activates the gripper, sets the action bit and
starts the move, with the speed and current last set by `#Gripvel` and `#Gripcur` (50 and 400 mA after power-up).

## The answer

Every Send_gripper_data_pack is answered with Respond_Gripper_data_pack, 4 bytes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Position | where the jaws are, 0 to 255 |
| Current | the motor current, mA; positive while opening, negative while closing |
| Activated | the activate flag |
| Action status | the action bit of the last command, as received; it stays 1 while the gripper holds, and the calibration does not change it |
| Object detection | 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position |
| Temperature error | the motor's thermistor is above the limit |
| Timeout error | the driver's CAN watchdog ran out |
| E-stop error | the E-stop bit was received |
| Calibrated | the gripper calibration is done |

The answer to a full command is sent before the gripper acts on that command, so it still carries the state from
before it; the answers to the polls that follow show the move. To follow a move, use the object detection: the
action status only repeats the bit you sent.

The bits are listed in [Errors and status bits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/errors/), with the byte layout in the
[CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/gripper/).

## A grip, message by message

What a host sends and what comes back, from power-up to a held object:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Host
    participant G as Gripper
    H->>G: Send_Clear_Error
    H->>G: Send_gripper_calibrate
    Note over G: the jaws open, pause, close: 0 and 255 are found
    loop only empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames, until calibrated
        H->>G: (0 bytes)
        G-->>H: answer: calibrated 0, at the end 1
    end
    H->>G: Send_gripper_data_pack(200, 30, 400, activate 1, action 1)
    G-->>H: answer: still the state from before the move
    loop every 20 ms, an empty Send_gripper_data_pack
        H->>G: (0 bytes)
        G-->>H: answer: position, current, state
    end
    G-->>H: answer: object found while closing (1), or at the position (3)
    Note over H: the grip is in, the next move waits for the program
```

## Object detection, exactly

While a move is in progress and the jaws are not yet at the target, the driver reads *moving* (0) as long as the
jaws move faster than 500 encoder ticks per second, about 1.6 mm/s. When they are slower than that and the motor
current is above 80 % of the commanded limit, something stops them: *object found*, 1 or 2 by the sign of the
current. Below 80 % with the jaws slow, it still reads *moving*: the object is soft and still being squeezed.
At the very start of a move the jaws are slow too, and with the current already near its limit the state can
briefly read 1 or 2; a host gives a move about 100 ms before it trusts the state. Once the target is reached, 3,
and it stays 3 until a different command arrives.

The state is therefore a snapshot of each answer. A host that wants to know "did the grip succeed" sends the move,
then polls until the state is 1, 2 or 3, with a timeout of its own; the ROS 2 driver and the PAROL6 software do
exactly that.

## What the current limit does

The current limit of a move is the driver's Iq limit for the duration of the move and the hold. It bounds the
torque, so the force on an object, and it also bounds how fast the jaws accelerate: a low limit with a high speed
gives a gentle, slow-starting move. The temperature of the motor is the other bound: holding an object at a high
current for minutes heats the windings, and at 75 °C the thermistor stops the gripper.

## Timing

The driver runs its loops at 6250 Hz; a move command takes effect at the next cycle, and the answer leaves within
a millisecond. The CAN bus at 1 Mbit/s carries a command and its answer in well under half a millisecond, so a host
can run the gripper at several hundred commands per second; 50 Hz is a good rate for a controller that polls the
state.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/can/ -->

# Over CAN

CAN is the gripper's interface: the one cable carries it next to the power, and a robot's control board, a PC with
the CANvas adapter or any microcontroller with a CAN transceiver drives the gripper with it. The gripper is a
STEPFOC driver on the bus, so the frames are the driver's; this page is the part a gripper needs.

## The frame

CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the
error state:

![Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/CANID.PNG){ width="600" }

- **Node ID**, bits 10 to 7: which device. Every gripper ships as node 0; set another with Send_CAN_ID or `#CANID`
  and save it. Use 0 to 13: the driver's bootloader reserves 14 and 15, and a device on one of those cannot be
  updated over CAN.
- **Command ID**, bits 6 to 1: which message. The gripper command is 61, its answer 60, the calibration 62.
- **Error bit**, bit 0: in a frame from the gripper, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is
  ignored.

So the gripper command to node 0 travels on identifier `(0 << 7) | (61 << 1)` = 0x7A, and the answer comes back on
`(60 << 1) | error` = 0x78 or 0x79; to node 3 the command is 0x1FA and the answer 0x1F8. Multi-byte values are
big-endian; flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

## The messages a gripper needs

| Message | ID | What for |
|---|---|---|
| [Send_gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_data_pack) | 61 | the move command: position, speed, current, the activate, action and E-stop bits; 0 bytes to poll |
| [Respond_Gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/gripper/#respond_gripper_data_pack) | 60 | the answer: position, current, the state and error bits |
| [Send_gripper_calibrate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/gripper/#send_gripper_calibrate) | 62 | the gripper calibration, after every power-up |
| [Send_Clear_Error](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_clear_error) | 1 | clears the errors |
| [Send_ESTOP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_estop), [Send_Idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_idle) | 0, 12 | stop |
| [Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_watchdog) | 15 | the gripper stops when the host stops talking |
| [Send_CAN_ID](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_can_id), [Send_Save_config](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/system/#send_save_config) | 11, 13 | another node ID, saved |
| [Send_Respond_State_of_Errors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/status/#send_respond_state_of_errors), [Send_Respond_Temperature](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/status/#send_respond_temperature) | 26, 23 | the driver's error flags, the motor temperature |

The [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/) has the bytes of each; the driver's other messages, which a
gripper does not need, are on the [STEPFOC site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/can/).

## A control loop

1. At power-up: Send_Clear_Error, then Send_gripper_calibrate; poll with empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames
   until the calibrated bit is 1 (up to about ten seconds; the routine gives up after 24 s). Send nothing else
   meanwhile.
2. For each grip: one Send_gripper_data_pack with the position, speed and current and the activate and action
   bits set. Its answer still carries the state from before it; ignore it. Then poll with empty frames until
   the object-detection field reads 1, 2 or 3, or your own timeout passes.
3. Keep polling at a steady rate (50 Hz is plenty) if you set the watchdog: every frame resets it, and the gripper
   stops by itself when your program stops.

The answer to every frame tells the whole state, so a host never has to ask twice.

## Host checklist

- **Clear, then calibrate.** With an error active, the driver drops the calibration request; a clear sent during
  the calibration ends it.
- **During the calibration, only empty frames.** A full Send_gripper_data_pack ends the calibration as well, and
  the gripper stays uncalibrated. Wait for the calibrated bit; the routine gives up after 24 s.
- **The first answer is old.** The answer to a full command is sent before the gripper acts on it. Ignore it,
  and give the move about 100 ms before you trust the object detection: at the start of a move the jaws are
  slow, which can briefly read as an object found.
- **The action status repeats your bit.** It is the action bit you last sent and stays 1 while the gripper
  holds. Follow a move by its object detection.
- **An identical command does nothing.** To repeat a move to the position the gripper holds, change the speed
  or the current by one.
- **E-stop recovery:** first a command with the E-stop bit at 0 (and the action bit at 0), then
  Send_Clear_Error. While the last command carries the E-stop bit, a clear does not hold.
- **Watchdog:** with Send_Watchdog set, keep the polls coming. The gripper commands and the status requests
  reset it; Send_Clear_Error and Send_gripper_calibrate do not. After a timeout, fix the host, clear, and
  resume.
- **Current:** keep the commanded current within the stepper's maximum, 1.5, 2.0 or 2.1 A; the firmware clamps
  it only at 2800 mA ([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)).

## From a PC

The [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) shows up as a serial port and
speaks slcan; `python-can` opens it with `bustype='slcan'`, and the [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/) wraps the messages.
Any CAN adapter that `python-can` supports works the same way.

## On a bus with other devices

A gripper on a robot shares the bus with the robot's joints or other grippers. Give each device its own node ID
(connect one at a time, Send_CAN_ID, Send_Save_config), terminate both ends of the bus
([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/can-termination/)), and keep in mind that a lower node ID wins the bus
arbitration.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/uart/ -->

# Over UART

The driver inside the gripper has a serial port. It is not the gripper's everyday interface, which is CAN, but it
is the way to configure the driver of a self-built gripper and the quickest way to look at what the driver
reports when something is wrong.

## Reaching the port

The UART connector of the driver (JST SH, 4 pins, 3.3 V) is inside the housing, under the coupler plate. Unscrew
the plate, plug in the [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) with
the UART cable, and open a terminal at 256000 baud with CR+LF line endings; the gripper's 24 V must be on for
anything but reading settings. [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/05-setup/terminal/)
on the STEPFOC site walks through the terminal setup.

!!! danger
    The port is 3.3 V. A 5 V adapter destroys the driver.

## The gripper commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `#Gripper 1` | gripper mode on (set and saved on every gripper); `#Gripper` prints it |
| `#Gripcal` | the gripper calibration |
| `#Gripvel 30` | the speed of the next moves, 0 to 255 |
| `#Gripcur 300` | the current limit of the next moves, mA |
| `#Grippos 200` | move to the position, 0 open to 255 closed; activates the gripper and starts the move |
| `#Gripact 1` | the activate flag without moving |
| `#Gripstop 1` | the E-stop bit |
| `#Gripinfo` | the gripper's state: calibrated, activated, the setpoints, the object detection, the end stops |

Only `#Grippos` starts a move. A session:

```
#Clear
#Gripcal
#Gripinfo
#Gripvel 30
#Gripcur 300
#Grippos 200
#Grippos 20
```

Wait until `#Gripinfo` reports the gripper calibrated before the first `#Grippos`: a `#Grippos` or a `#Clear`
during the calibration ends it. After `#Gripstop 1`, send `#Gripstop 0` before `#Clear`, or the E-stop error
comes straight back.

The [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/uart/) has these and the driver commands a gripper needs; the driver's
whole command set is on the [STEPFOC site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/reference/uart/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/ -->

# With Python

The `Spectral-BLDC` library wraps the driver's CAN protocol, gripper messages included: one method per message,
and the gripper's answers unpacked into attributes. The ROS 2 driver and the legacy gripper GUI are built on it.

## Installing

In a virtual environment, with Python 3.10 or newer:

=== "Windows"
    ```
    py -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    pip install Spectral-BLDC
    ```
    The CANvas adapter's port is `COM` and a number: Device Manager lists it under **Ports (COM & LPT)**. Give it
    as `channel='COM20'`.

=== "Linux"
    ```
    python3 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    pip install Spectral-BLDC
    sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER     # access to the adapter's port; log out and in again once
    ```
    The adapter's port is `/dev/ttyACM0` (`ls /dev/ttyACM*` lists it).

=== "macOS"
    ```
    python3 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    pip install Spectral-BLDC
    ```
    The adapter's port is `/dev/tty.usbmodem` and a number (`ls /dev/tty.usbmodem*` lists it).

The library pulls `python-can` and `pyserial`. The source and the examples are in
[Spectral-BLDC-Python](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/Spectral-BLDC-Python).

## The first program

```python
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM20 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
bus = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM20', bitrate=1000000)
gripper = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=bus)

gripper.Send_Clear_Error()                      # clear first: with an error active, the calibration does not run
gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()                # the jaws open fully, then close fully
for _ in range(120):                            # wait for the calibrated bit, up to 24 s
    time.sleep(0.2)
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack()            # only empty frames now: a move or a clear ends the calibration
    message, ids = bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.05)
    if message is not None:
        gripper.UnpackData(message, ids)
        if gripper.gripper_calibrated:
            break

for position in (200, 20, 200, 20):
    # position 0..255, speed 0..255, current mA, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(position, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.05)      # its answer still carries the state from before the move
    time.sleep(0.1)                             # give the move time to start
    for _ in range(40):                         # poll the state for up to 2 s
        gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack()        # an empty frame: status only
        message, ids = bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.05)
        if message is not None:
            gripper.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(gripper.gripper_position, gripper.gripper_current, gripper.gripper_object_detection)
            if gripper.gripper_object_detection in (1, 2, 3):   # object found, or at the position
                break
```

The answer to a move command is sent before the gripper acts on it, so it still carries the state from before:
after a finished move, object detection 3. The example reads that answer and drops it. At the very start of a
move the jaws are still slow, and with the current near its limit the object detection can briefly read 1 or 2;
the pause of 0.1 s covers that. While the gripper calibration runs, send only empty frames: a full command or
Send_Clear_Error ends the calibration, and the gripper stays uncalibrated.

`Send_gripper_data_pack` with all seven arguments sends the move; without arguments it sends the empty status
poll. `receive_can_messages` returns the raw `python-can` message and the node ID, command ID and error bit from
the identifier; `UnpackData` fills the gripper attributes:

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gripper_position` | 0 open to 255 closed |
| `gripper_current` | the motor current in mA |
| `gripper_activated`, `gripper_action_status` | the activate flag; the action bit of the last command, which stays 1 while the gripper holds |
| `gripper_object_detection` | 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position |
| `gripper_temperature_error`, `gripper_timeout_error`, `gripper_estop_error` | the three error bits |
| `gripper_calibrated` | the gripper calibration is done |

!!! note "Object detection in library 1.20 and older"
    Library 1.20 and older assemble `gripper_object_detection` with its two bits swapped relative to the firmware:
    they report 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object found while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object found
    while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. 1.21 and newer read them right. The example tests for "1 or 2", which
    is right with every version.

## Stopping

```python
gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 1, 0)   # the E-stop bit: stops, raises the E-stop error
gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 0, 0, 0)   # to recover: first the bit back at 0, action 0
gripper.Send_Clear_Error()                                 # then clear; while the bit is 1, the error comes back
gripper.Send_Watchdog(500)                                 # from now on the gripper stops 500 ms after the last frame
```

With the watchdog set, keep the status poll running at a steady rate; a program that crashes releases the grip
within the watchdog time.

## Several grippers

One `CanCommunication` per bus, one `SpectralCAN` per gripper with its node ID; every answer carries the node ID
in `ids.node_id`, so route it to the right object. The [teleoperation guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/guides/teleoperation/) couples
two grippers this way.

The complete map of calls to messages is in the [Python library](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/python/) reference.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ros2/ -->

# With ROS 2

The [msg_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2) package is a ROS 2
Humble driver for the gripper, built on the Python library and a `python-can` adapter. It was developed by the
UCLA Biomechatronics Lab and Ben Forbes, and is MIT licensed.

## What it offers

| Direction | Topic or action | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Command | `/gripper/command_joint_states` | `sensor_msgs/JointState`, the position as the gripper's own units, 0 to 255 |
| Feedback | `/gripper/feedback_joint_states` | `sensor_msgs/JointState`, the position in the same units and the effort in mA |
| Action | `/gripper_command` | `control_msgs/GripperCommand` |

## Installing

Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 or newer, and a USB-to-CAN adapter that speaks slcan, such as the
CANvas:

```bash
pip install Spectral_BLDC python-can
cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2.git
cd ~/ros2_ws
colcon build --packages-select msg_gripper_ros2
source install/setup.bash
```

On Linux, add yourself to the `dialout` group to open the adapter's port without `sudo`, and log in again.

## Running

```bash
ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py
```

The only setting that depends on your machine is the adapter's port, `channel` in `config/default.yaml`:
`/dev/ttyACM0` or `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux, `/dev/tty.usbmodem*` on macOS, `COM3` on Windows. Copy the file,
change it, and pass it at launch:

```bash
ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py config_file:=~/my_gripper.yaml node_name:=my_gripper namespace:=robot
```

The package's README has the rest: the parameters, the node names, and the platforms it was tested on.

## The SSG-48 package

The [ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Lass6230/ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2)
package, written for the SSG-48 gripper, speaks the same protocol and should work with the MSG as well.

## The description files

The gripper's standalone URDF and MJCF (MuJoCo) packages, with solid or soft TPU jaws, come from
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions); the product repository's
[msg_description](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/msg_description) guide links the
downloads and says how to open them. Its display launch file is for ROS 1; in ROS 2, load the URDF with a launch
file of your own.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/ -->

# On PAROL6 and PAR6

The gripper is made for the Source Robotics arms. Both drive it over their own CAN bus; their software calibrates
it, moves it and reads its state, so a program for the robot does not talk CAN itself. What any robot's software
needs to carry the gripper, the tool centre point, the mass, the centre of mass and the inertia, is on
[Data for robot integration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/integration-data/).

## PAROL6

### Mounting and connecting

1. Replace the gripper's `ring_cover` with `ring_cover-PAROL6` from the STEP files' `Common parts`
   ([Mounting on a robot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/mounting/)). It bolts to the robot's last joint, and the coupler
   plate's shaft coupler (8 mm bore, two M4 clamp screws) takes the joint 6 shaft.
2. Slide the gripper onto the shaft with the camera looking down between the jaws, and tighten the two clamp
   screws with blue threadlocker.
3. Connect the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) between the gripper and
   the M8 connector at the forearm. Only this cable: the PAR6 cable is wired differently and destroys the gripper
   ([The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/)).
4. Route the camera's USB cable outside the arm, with slack for joints 4, 5 and 6, and fix it so that the arm
   cannot catch it.
5. Keep the gripper's node ID at 0 and set its termination switch ON; it is the last node on the robot's bus.

### The joint 5 homing offset

Joint 5 homes against the tool, and the control board firmware's default offset (8900) is for the pneumatic
gripper holder, not for the MSG's ring cover. After the first homing, check joint 5 with the pin through its
witness marks. If it is off, measure the offset and set `j5_homing_offset` in `main.cpp` of the control board
firmware, as the PAROL6 documentation's mastering page describes.

### Driving it

The gripper calibrates after every power-up and does not move before that. Clear the gripper's errors first, then
calibrate, then wait until the calibration is done, up to about ten seconds: a gripper move or a clear sent while
it runs ends the calibration.

=== "Commander software"
    The **Gripper** tab: after homing the robot, press **Clear gripper error**, then **Calibrate gripper**, and
    wait until the status says calibrated. Then set the position, speed and current with the sliders and press
    **Move GoTo**. In RBTscript: `Gripper_cal()`, `Delay(10)`, then `Gripper(position, speed, current)`, with the
    current in mA.

=== "Python API"
    ```python
    import time

    rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")           # the parol6 package; 100mm, 150mm or 200mm: the rail
    rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # with the robot at rest
    time.sleep(10)                                         # the calibration takes up to about ten seconds
    rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions; current 0.4 is 1180 mA
    print(rbt.tool.status())
    ```

    The API allows the calibration 2 s before it sends the next gripper action, which is too short for the MSG;
    the pause above waits for the calibration to finish.

The Python API's `current` is a fraction of the range 100 to 2800 mA: the gripper gets 100 + 2700 × `current` mA,
so 1.0 is 2800 mA, more than any of the steppers takes. Keep it within the stepper's maximum
([Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)):

| Stepper | Maximum current | Largest `current` |
|---|---|---|
| 21.5 mm | 1.5 A | 0.51 |
| 40 mm | 2.0 A | 0.70 |
| 60 mm | 2.1 A | 0.74 |

`position` and `speed` are fractions of the position and speed bytes: 0.8 is position 204, 0.5 is speed 128.

The [PAROL6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/) covers the robot's side: the gripper
port, the commander software, the API and the tool centre point.

## PAR6

The PAR6 arm's control box runs the gripper on its CAN bus as a tool, with the PAR6 gripper cable (different from
the PAROL6 one). The [PAR6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/) covers the tool configuration,
the runtime's gripper commands and the firmware updates the box can do for the gripper.

## Another robot

Any controller with a CAN interface drives the gripper directly: [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/can/) is the protocol,
[With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/) and [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/ros2/) are two ready implementations, and the
[CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/reference/can/) has every byte.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/ -->

# Errors and recovery

When the driver inside the gripper detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle and sets the error bit in
every CAN frame it sends. The grip is released: an idle stepper holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction.

## Seeing the error

- **The error bit** of every answer's identifier: 1 while any error is active.
- **Respond_Gripper_data_pack** carries the three gripper error bits: temperature, timeout, E-stop.
- **Send_Respond_State_of_Errors** returns every flag of the driver, which is where the other causes show.
- Motor GUI shows the errors in its gripper panel; `#Error` over UART prints them.

## The errors

| Error | Reported in | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature | the gripper's temperature bit | the thermistor on the motor housing reads more than 75 °C (`#Tlim`) | let the motor cool; hold with less current |
| Timeout | the gripper's timeout bit | the driver's CAN watchdog ran out: no valid frame within the time set by Send_Watchdog | the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear |
| E-stop | the gripper's E-stop bit | a move command with the E-stop bit set, or `#Gripstop 1` | send a command with the bit at 0 (or `#Gripstop 0`), then clear: while the last command's bit is 1, a clear does not hold |
| Not calibrated (motor) | State_of_Errors, `#Error` | the driver's own motor calibration is missing: a self-built gripper before [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/), or after `#Default` | calibrate the motor |
| Vbus | State_of_Errors | the supply is below 9 V or above the driver's `#Vmax` limit, 29 V after `#Default` | the supply, the cable |
| Encoder | State_of_Errors | the driver's encoder does not see its magnet | the magnet on the stepper shaft (a self-built gripper) |
| Driver | State_of_Errors | the driver stage's own protection tripped: overcurrent, overtemperature | lower the current; check the motor leads |
| Velocity | State_of_Errors | the motor exceeded the driver's speed limit | unlikely in a gripper; clear |
| Driver E-stop | State_of_Errors | Send_ESTOP was received | clear |

A gripper that is not **gripper-calibrated** is not in error: it just refuses moves until Send_gripper_calibrate
has found the end stops.

## Clearing

Send_Clear_Error, **Clear** in the GUI or `#Clear` clears every flag, the gripper's E-stop included, and goes to
idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back: a hot motor, a supply that is still low.

The gripper's E-stop counts as such a cause while the E-stop bit of the last gripper command is 1: the driver
raises the error again at every cycle. So after an E-stop, first send a gripper command with the E-stop bit at 0
and the action bit at 0 (or `#Gripstop 0` over UART), then clear. The next command with the action bit set moves
the gripper again.

After clearing, the gripper is idle and still calibrated and activated; the next move command moves it. A clear
sent while the gripper calibration runs ends the calibration, and the gripper stays uncalibrated.

## When the gripper does not answer

- No answer at all: the supply, the cable (and its pinout), the bus termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL
  with everything unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter, the node ID.
- Answers but does not move: not calibrated, not activated, an error active, or the action bit at 0.
- Moves to one end during calibration and stops there: the other end stop is blocked, or the mechanism is too
  stiff for the calibration's 500 mA; after 24 seconds the routine gives up.

[Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/) goes through the symptoms one by one.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/07-maintenance/ -->

# Maintenance

The gripper needs little: every wearing part is printed, so a worn part is replaced by printing a new one, and
the mechanism is a rail, two racks and a pinion that want a little grease now and then. Power the gripper off
before any work on it. Before you open the stepper cover or touch the driver, unplug the supply and touch earthed
metal: static electricity damages the driver board. Hold the board by its edges.

## Before each session

- The jaws sit tight on their carriers, nothing is cracked, the pads or the sponge tape are whole.
- The cable's M8 nut is tight, the cable has slack for the wrist's full motion and runs clear of the jaws.
- Nothing lies in the jaws' travel, and the gripper calibration finds both end stops.

## When the motion gets rough, and every few months of regular use

- **Grease.** A little lithium grease on the rail and on the rack and pinion. Remove the four screws that hold
  the linear rail to reach the mechanism, wipe off the old grease and the dust, grease, refit, and move the jaws
  over the whole stroke by hand before you power up. A grinding noise, a stiff motion or a calibration that
  stops short of an end are the signs that it is due.
- **Clean** the rail and the racks of chips and dust, as [Cleaning](#cleaning) describes.
- **Screws**: the jaw screws, the rail screws and the clamp screws of the shaft coupler; threadlocker where the
  assembly instructions use it.
- **The camera lens**, with a lens cloth.

## Cleaning

Clean the gripper switched off and unplugged. Wipe the printed parts with a dry or slightly damp cloth, or with a little isopropyl
alcohol on the cloth for grease; use no other solvents, such as acetone: the body is PETG, the pads are TPU. Never spray or pour anything onto the gripper; the driver
behind the stepper cover and the M8 connector are open to it, and it is not waterproof or dustproof. Brush or blow
chips out of the rail and the racks rather than wash them out, then grease them as above.

## Replacing worn parts

The jaws, the pads and every other printed part are in the product repository,
[Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files); the
rail, the carriages, the pinion and the screws are in the
[BOM](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/BOM.md). A replacement jaw
is the same part as a new one, and the gripper calibration at the next power-up takes care of the end stops.

A stepper or a driver is not serviced but replaced: the stepper by one of the three in the BOM, after which the
motor calibration of [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/) is run again; the driver by a new
[STEPFOC driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-stepper-controller), configured the same way.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/08-firmware/ -->

# Firmware

The gripper has no firmware of its own: it runs the STEPFOC driver's firmware with gripper mode turned on. This
site describes the firmware release named in the version box on the landing page, for the gripper release the
site is versioned by; a new firmware release for the same gripper updates these pages in place.

## Which release does my gripper run?

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Device_Info returns the firmware version as its third byte; over UART, `#Info` prints
`Software version: <number>`. The [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/appendix/compatibility/) says which releases go with
which Python library and bootloader.

## Updating

A gripper whose driver runs firmware 105 or newer carries the driver's bootloader and updates over its CAN cable: the
host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image
into it. Nothing is opened. The image is `stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin` from the driver's
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/releases), with a manifest
`firmware.json` and the release notes.

| From | How |
|---|---|
| a PC with the CANvas adapter | [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) over CAN: choose the release, the GUI fetches the image and flashes it |
| a PC, scripted | `host_tools/bl_flash.py` from the [bootloader repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader), over CAN (slcan or gs_usb adapters) or over the driver's UART port |
| a PAR6 control box | the box updates every device on its bus, the gripper included, from its dashboard or `tools/flash_motor_firmware.py` |

The procedure, the bootloader's protocol and what to do when a flash is interrupted are in the STEPFOC
documentation: [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/update/)
and [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/the-bootloader/).

!!! warning "Before you update"
    - Open the gripper or take the object out: it loses its grip during the update and until it is calibrated
      and commanded again.
    - An update may clear the driver's configuration (the release notes say so when it does). A bought gripper's
      configuration is in [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/), so it can be restored; note
      what `#Info` prints before you start.
    - Give the gripper a node ID from 0 to 13: the bootloader cannot address 14 or 15.

!!! success "Check"
    After the update, `#Info` prints `Software version:` with the new release (over CAN, the third byte of
    Send_Respond_Device_Info), and the gripper calibrates and moves as before. If it no longer answers as a
    gripper, its configuration was cleared: restore it as in [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/).

A gripper whose driver runs firmware 103 or older has no bootloader; it is updated once with a programming
adapter on the driver's JTAG pads, inside the housing, as described in
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/latest/07-firmware/bootloader/).
From then on it updates over CAN like any other.

## Release notes

The release notes of every STEPFOC release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix,
[Firmware release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/appendix/firmware-release-notes/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/ -->

# Troubleshooting

By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/); the
faults in the firmware and the software that are known and not yet fixed, with what to do until they are, are in
[Known issues](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/known-issues/).

## The gripper does not answer

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| nothing at all | the 24 V on the cable; the cable's pinout (a wrong one has destroyed the driver already); the node ID the host uses; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; the termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL, unpowered) |
| answers, then stops answering | the watchdog ran out and the host did not notice; a loose M8 connector; a second device with the same node ID |
| the GUI shows *No connection* | the COM port of the CANvas adapter; another program holding the port; the CAN ID in the GUI |

## It does not move

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([The gripper does not move]) --> B{Does it answer on CAN?}
    B -- no --> C[24 V on the cable, the pinout, the node ID,<br>1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[Run the gripper calibration;<br>a self-built gripper: the stepper calibration first]
    D -- yes --> F{An error flag set?}
    F -- yes --> G[Clear it; if it comes back,<br>Errors and recovery names the cause]
    F -- no --> H{Activate and action bits at 1?}
    H -- no --> I[Send the command with activate = 1 and action = 1]
    H -- yes --> J[The command equals the previous one:<br>change the speed or the current by one]
```

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| calibrated, activated, no error, no motion | the action bit of the command is 0; the command is identical to the previous one (change the speed or the current by one to repeat a move) |
| *Not calibrated* after power-up | normal: run the gripper calibration |
| an error is shown | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/): clear it, then look at the cause if it comes back |
| the driver reports *Not calibrated* in State_of_Errors and `#Error` | the stepper itself is not calibrated (a self-built gripper): [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/) |

## Calibration

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| the jaws move to one end and stop; after 24 s the gripper is still not calibrated | the other end is blocked, or the mechanism is too stiff for the calibration's 500 mA: a tight rail, a pinion pressed too hard into the racks, debris in the racks |
| the jaws jitter and do not travel | a phase of the stepper not connected (self-built), or the stepper not calibrated |
| 255 is not fully closed, or 0 not fully open | something stopped the jaws short of the end during calibration; calibrate again with the stroke free |

## The grip

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| the object slips | the current too low for the object; the jaw faces: sponge tape or the TPU pad |
| the object is crushed | the current too high; a hard object takes the full force at once |
| *object detected* while nothing is there | the current limit too low for the mechanism's friction at that speed; raise the current a little or lower the speed |
| the gripper stops with a temperature error after a while | a long hold at a high current; hold with the lowest current that keeps the object |
| the jaws creep or hum when holding | the position loop against a hard object; lower the current, or hold a soft object with a position slightly beyond the contact |

## Noise and heat

A stepper under field-oriented control is quiet; a grinding noise is the rack and pinion without grease, or
debris. The motor gets warm in use and hot under a long grip; the thermistor stops it at 75 °C. A self-built
gripper without the thermistor on its motor has no such protection.

## After a firmware update

If the gripper does not calibrate or behaves oddly after an update, check the driver's configuration over UART:
`#Gripper` (gripper mode, 1), `#Term` (the thermistor, 1) and `#Info` (the motor calibration and parameters). A
release note says when an update clears the configuration; [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/) restores
it.

## Getting help

[Support](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/support/) says where to ask and what to include; the gripper's status and `#Info`'s output are
the first things.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/known-issues/ -->

# Known issues

The faults in the gripper's firmware and in the software that drives it that are known and not yet fixed, and
what to do until they are. The pages that describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects
them in one place. Which versions work together is in [Versions and compatibility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/appendix/compatibility/).

### STEPFOC firmware

Seen in: 109 (the driver's firmware, gripper mode).

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-1 | After a gripper command with the E-stop bit set, the E-stop error comes back at every control cycle for as long as the last gripper command carries the bit, so a clear seems to do nothing. | First send a gripper command with the E-stop bit at 0 and the action bit at 0 (`#Gripstop 0` over UART), then clear. | [Errors and recovery, clearing](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/errors/#clearing) |
| KI-2 | The answer to a full gripper command is sent before the gripper acts on it, so it carries the state from before the command, for example object detection 3 of the move before. | Ignore that answer. Poll with empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames, and give a move about 100 ms before you trust its object detection. | [How the gripper works, the answer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/#the-answer) |
| KI-3 | A full gripper command or a clear sent while the gripper calibration runs ends it, and the gripper stays uncalibrated. The routine's progress and its 24 s timer are not reset, so the next calibration can start part way through or give up early. | Clear first, then calibrate, and send only empty status polls until the calibrated bit is 1. After an interrupted calibration, switch the gripper off and on before you calibrate again. | [How the gripper works, the states](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/#the-states) |
| KI-4 | The action status in the gripper's answer is the action bit of the last command as it was received; the gripper never clears it, so it stays 1 after a move has finished and while the gripper holds. | Follow a move by its object detection (0 moving, 1 or 2 object found, 3 at the position), not by the action status. | [How the gripper works, the answer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/how-it-works/#the-answer) |

### PAROL6 Python API (parol6)

Seen in: 0.9.1.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-7 | `tool.status()` does not follow the gripper's status byte: `engaged` reads true at all times, and `part_detected` comes from bits 3 and 2 of the byte, which hold the temperature and timeout errors, not the object detection. The calibrated and error bits are not in it. | Use the jaw position (`positions`) and the current (`channels`), and check where the jaws stopped to know that a part is held. | [On PAROL6 and PAR6, driving it](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/#driving-it) |
| KI-8 | `calibrate()` counts the calibration done after a fixed 2 s without reading the calibrated bit; the next gripper action then ends a calibration that is still running, and the MSG's takes up to about ten seconds. The API has no action that clears the gripper's errors. | Wait about 10 s after `calibrate()` before the next gripper action. Clear a gripper error with the commander's **Clear gripper error** or with Motor GUI, then calibrate. | [On PAROL6 and PAR6, driving it](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/#driving-it) |
| KI-9 | The MSG's `current` is a fraction of 100 to 2800 mA, so `current=1.0` commands 2800 mA, more than any of the three steppers takes, and the firmware clamps only above 2800 mA. | Keep `current` at or below 0.51 (21.5 mm stepper), 0.70 (40 mm) or 0.74 (60 mm). | [On PAROL6 and PAR6, driving it](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/robots/#driving-it) |

### Fixed

| | What happened | Fixed in | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-5 | The motor calibration (`#Cal`) leaves the driver's current limit at 1600 mA, whatever it was before, which is more than the 21.5 mm stepper's 1.5 A. Gripper moves use the current of each command; the limit applies when the driver runs as a motor (Motor GUI's Motor side, the UART motor modes). | 109: calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started | [Driver setup, current limit](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/#current-limit) |
| KI-6 | `UnpackData` assembles `gripper_object_detection` with its two bits swapped: it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object found while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object found while closing); 0 and 3 are right. | 1.21: `UnpackData` reads the two bits the right way round | [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/python/#the-first-program) |
| KI-10 | A status poll (an empty Send_gripper_data_pack) or a repeat of the command that reaches the driver within one control cycle (about 0.16 ms) of a new move command cancels it as new. The move then runs in position mode, and object detection reads 3 while the jaws press on an object. | 109: only a new command marks itself new, so a poll or a repeat no longer cancels the move | [Over CAN, host checklist](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/06-operation/can/#host-checklist) |

## Something that is not here

Check [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/) first. If it is still not explained,
[Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/support/report-a-problem/) says what to include so it can be reproduced. A fixed issue
stays on this page, under "Fixed", with the version that fixes it.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/ -->

# Build guide

**The MSG is open source, and that is important to us.** Everything the gripper is made of is published in the
[product repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper) under the CERN Open
Hardware Licence: the STEP and print files of every part, the bill of materials with a link for every item, the
assembly video, and the URDF and MJCF models. The driver's firmware and the software that drives the gripper are
open source too. A gripper you build is the same gripper as the one from the shop, and this manual applies to
it; change the jaws, the camera mount or the body for your application, or fit the gripper to a robot it was not
designed for. This guide is the order to do it in.

!!! warning
    A self-built gripper is yours to make safe: the thermistor on the motor, the current within the stepper's
    maximum, and the [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/02-safety/) chapter apply to it as to a bought one. The gripper is in beta:
    expect rough edges in the hardware and the software.

## The steps

1. Choose a rail length for the stroke and a stepper length for the force: [Variants](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/01-overview/variants/).
2. [Bill of materials](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/bill-of-materials/): the repository's BOM, with the reference images.
3. [Printing the parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/printing/): PETG at 25 % infill, the folders for your rail and stepper, the jaws.
4. [Mechanical assembly](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/mechanical-assembly/): the video, the order, the cable.
5. [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/): the motor calibration before the pinion goes in, gripper mode,
   the thermistor, the first moves.

## Kits and the shop

You do not have to source everything yourself:

| | What is in it | You add |
|---|---|---|
| [STEPFOC starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-starter-kit) | the STEPFOC driver, the CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter, the USB-to-serial adapter, an ST-Link with the programming adapter, the UART, power and CAN cables, the 6 × 2.5 mm encoder magnet, the 100K thermistor | the stepper, the rail and its carriages, the pinion, the shaft coupler, the M8 connector, the screws and inserts, the camera, the printed parts |
| [STEPFOC driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/stepfoc-stepper-controller) alone | the driver | the rest, and the adapters its setup needs |
| [Assembled MSG gripper](https://source-robotics.com/products/msg-gripper) | the gripper, built, calibrated and configured, in the rail, stepper and colour you choose | the [cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) |

The starter kit is the good-value start for a build: it has the driver and everything the driver's setup needs,
the CAN adapter for Motor GUI, the serial adapter for the UART, the magnet, the thermistor and the two internal
cables, for little more than the driver alone. The [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable)
is in the shop too.

# Bill of materials

!!! note "This is a copy"
    The original is [BOM.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/BOM.md) in the gripper's repository; this page is that file as of
    2026-10-31 (commit `9862f62`), with the reference images shown inline. If a link is broken or a part is wrong,
    [open an issue](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/issues/new) there, and the fix lands here with the next sync. The shop's
    [starter kit](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/#kits-and-the-shop) covers the driver and everything its setup needs.

This BOM lists all components required to build the MSG gripper. Quantities are for **one gripper**.

!!! note
    If any product links are broken, unavailable, or no longer point to the correct item, please [open an issue](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/issues/new), send us a message on Discord, or contact us via email. You can also use the reference images to find the same or an equivalent part from another supplier.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/printing/ -->

# Printing the parts

## Material and settings

PETG for every part but the TPU jaw pads. The repository's print table is one line, and it is the whole rule:
**use 25 % infill for all** ([Print_table.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Print_table.md)).
Supports where your slicer asks for them; the body prints on its back.

## The files

| Variant | Folders in [STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files) |
|---|---|
| every gripper | [`Common parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Common%20parts): the coupler plate and ring cover (or `ring_cover-PAROL6`), the camera mount and lid, the jaw blocker, the stepper spacer, the connector lid |
| your rail | [`Linear rail dependant parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Linear%20rail%20dependant%20parts)`/<rail>`: the body and the two jaw carriers |
| your stepper | [`Stepper dependant parts`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20dependant%20parts)`/<stepper>`: the stepper cover, and the spacer for the 21.5 mm stepper |
| the jaws | [`Gripper jaws attachment`](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Gripper%20jaws%20attachment): one of the designs, mirrored for the other side |

The [Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files)
folder has the same parts as 3MF, ready to slice.

## The jaws

Two kinds, both in `Gripper jaws attachment`; mirror the file in the slicer for the other side, except the solid
jaw, which has a mirrored file:

- **TPU jaws** (recommended): a PETG body, `MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE`, and a soft TPU pad printed separately and glued
  on. The pad deforms around the object for a gentler, surer grip. Print the pad with **16 % infill, no top or
  bottom layers and 2 walls** for the softest grip; the body with the normal settings.
- **Solid jaws**: `MSG_solid_jaw` and `MSG_solid_jaw_mirror` in one piece, or `MSG_JAW_HOLLOW` for a two-colour
  print; `MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE` prints solid too.

![The TPU jaw in the slicer: the PETG body (orange) and the TPU pad (green) as separate parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/jaw_slicer1.webp){ width="520" }

![Two TPU pads sliced with the pad's settings: the honeycomb infill shows, with no top layer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/assets/jaw_slicer2.webp){ width="520" }

Gluing the pad on, its orientation and the sponge tape for the gripping faces are in
[Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/); the repository's
[jaw guide](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Building_gripper_jaws.md)
is the original.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/mechanical-assembly/ -->

# Mechanical assembly

The assembly is shown in the repository's video; a PDF manual is in preparation. Watch the video once before you
start, with the parts in front of you.

<iframe width="100%" height="460" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/EosuDy-heqM" title="MSG gripper assembly" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe>

[Open the video on YouTube](https://youtu.be/EosuDy-heqM)

## The order

Touch earthed metal before you pick up the driver, and hold it by its edges: static electricity damages it.

1. The driver first: calibrated, in gripper mode, with the thermistor, as [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/first-run/)
   describes. The motor calibration turns the stepper several revolutions, which the racks cannot follow, so it
   happens before the pinion meshes.
2. The brass inserts into the printed parts with a soldering iron.
3. The rail with its two carriages into the body, the racks onto the carriers.
4. The stepper, with the pinion on its shaft and the driver on its back, into the body so that the pinion meshes
   with both racks; the thermistor's leads to the driver.
5. The driver's power and CAN cables to the M8 connector in its lid; the lid onto the body.
6. The stepper cover over the driver, with the termination switch reachable through its opening.
7. The coupler plate with the shaft coupler on the back, or `ring_cover-PAROL6` for the PAROL6 wrist.
8. The jaws onto the carriers, the camera into its mount.

!!! success "Check"
    With the supply off, push one jaw by hand over the whole stroke: both jaws move together, smoothly, without a
    tight spot, and nothing rubs on the cable. The termination switch is reachable through the stepper cover.
    A stiff spot now makes the gripper calibration stop short later
    ([Calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/09-troubleshooting/#calibration)).

## The cable

The gripper's cable is not in the box. [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/cable/) has the parts, the wiring
diagrams for PAROL6 and PAR6, and the warning that the two are not interchangeable; the repository's
[cable guide](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/MSG-compliant-AI-stepper-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Building_cables.md)
is the original.

## The jaws

Printing, gluing and padding the jaws: [Printing the parts](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/build/printing/) and [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/1.2/04-installation/jaws/).
